_transcript: What happens when an entire generation of people cannot enter a job market because entry-level jobs have collapsed? People don't understand that entry-level jobs provide so much more than just like a initial income. They also give young workers the chance to learn by doing. The implicit bargain is very much breaking down because of AI and it's also reshaping the idea of what entry level even means. The unemployment rate for college graduates is very high. Entry-level job postings is very low, especially in industries like tech and marketing and finance. You know, precisely those white collar fields where Gen Z graduates expected to build their careers. Like that's kind of what they went to college for. And, you know, we're seeing how companies are discovering and like, oh, AI can handle these tasks that maybe they traditionally assign to junior employees. And of course, this creates a potential paradox that's only going to get worse. You know, employers still want experienced mid-level candidates, but those candidates eventually have to come from somewhere. So if those entry points disappear, so does the pipeline of future talent. We're essentially pulling up the ladder behind us. And the consequences extend beyond, like the individual. You know, young people locked out of career track jobs are losing income, yes, but they're also losing the skills that come with working alongside experienced colleagues. You know, how do you learn some of the soft skills like navigating office politics, handling difficult conversations from a YouTube tutorial? I mean, so much of this is very much learned by doing. And so then what happens when young people don't have access to that? We already are starting to see a response in young people, you know, pivoting towards entrepreneurship, freelancing, credential stacking. But that might not translate in the same way as other types of entry-level jobs. And also, not everyone has the resources or risk tolerance to do that. And so a labor market that only rewards those who can self-fund their own training or go off on their own or have the backing to do that will just continue to deepen those inequalities.

_transcript: Is AI bad for the environment? Let's fact check, because you've probably seen stats like AI will use more electricity than Japan by 2030, or that it uses millions of litres of water. And that's possibly true, but there's a bit more to it. So each simple prompt in something like ChatGPT uses about a third of a watt hour, whereas if you boil a kettle, that uses about 100 watt hours, which is 300 times as much as a simple ChatGPT question. But not all AI queries are equal. These newer reasoning and agent-like AI models, the ones that sit there thinking for ages before they answer, Claude Cowork, Claude Code, etc., they can use over 33 watt hours for a single prompt. That's 100 times more than a simple one. So the way that you use AI matters quite a lot, but also the way you use the internet matters. Because remember that streaming just five seconds of video somewhere like Netflix uses about the same energy as a simple ChatGPT prompt. So on a personal level, your AI use is negligible. But the real impact is what happens before that technology reaches you. You know, what went into building it, right? Because there's the training of AI, which has been estimated to use as much energy as about 120 homes use in a year just to train one model. And then there's the data centers that they have to build to run these things. And we talking about huge facilities that cover hundreds of acres and they need colossal amounts of concrete and steel to build them And we know that concrete and steel and construction have a huge environmental impact like cement production alone is responsible for about eight percent of all global carbon emissions and then you got diesel powered construction equipment on top of that land being cleared ecosystems being disrupted and that is land that will never be farmland or forest or anything else ever again and then there's water so data centers generate huge amount of heat as you can imagine like when your computer gets busy it gets hot but it's like that on a massive scale and most of them cool their servers by running water through cooling towers where that evaporates into the air and that gets rid of the heat. But of course, 80% of that water is just lost to evaporation and that water is drawn from local freshwater supplies. That's the same supply that serves homes and farms. Google alone apparently used 31 billion litres of water across its data centres in 2024 and that can only go up, right? And when these data centres get built in areas already dealing with drought, that obviously creates real conflict, real problems in those local communities, which is not good. So the way I see it is the global impact is way bigger than people realise, but the per person impact is way smaller. And that's something we've all got to reconcile. It's a very personal decision. Like right now, today, you can have a much bigger impact on the environment by not eating meat, flying less, buying and consuming less stuff than abstaining from AI. But at the same time, how do we put pressure on the AI companies to reduce their impact on this absolutely huge scale?

description: AI is moving fast, and I think a lot of people are still underestimating how much it could change the job market over the next few years. Some people believe AI will mostly be a tool that helps workers become faster, smarter, and more productive. Others think it will replace entire categories of jobs, especially work that is repetitive, predictable, or easy to automate. The truth is probably somewhere in the middle, but that middle may still be a huge disruption for millions of people. What makes this conversation interesting is that AI does not have to replace a whole profession overnight to have a major impact. It can slowly take over pieces of jobs first. Maybe it writes reports faster, answers customer questions, generates content, summarizes meetings, reviews contracts, handles scheduling, or helps with coding and research. Once enough pieces of a role are automated, companies may decide they need fewer people to do the same amount of work. That is where a lot of concern comes from. At the same time, there is another side to this. People who learn how to use AI well may become more valuable, not less. Someone who understands their field and knows how to combine real experience with AI tools could outperform people who refuse to adapt. In that way, AI may not just replace workers. It may widen the gap between people who embrace it early and people who ignore it until it is too late. I also think the impact will not be the same for every job. Some careers that involve hands-on work, human trust, real-world problem solving, leadership, creativity with taste and judgment, or complex decision-making may hold up better than jobs built mostly around repeatable digital tasks. But even those jobs could still change a lot. The way people work, the skills employers want, and the value of certain experience may all shift faster than many expect. A lot of people used to think this kind of disruption was far away. Now it feels like it is already starting. Students are using AI. Businesses are using AI. Employers are experimenting with AI. Creators are using AI. Programmers are using AI. Customer service teams are using AI. Marketing teams are using AI. That does not automatically mean mass replacement happens tomorrow, but it does mean the conversation is no longer hypothetical. So I am curious what other people think. Is AI actually coming for jobs, or is it mostly going to become another tool people use every day like the internet, smartphones, or search engines? Will it mainly replace low-skill tasks, or do you think white-collar jobs are more at risk than people realize? Are trades and hands-on careers safer? Will companies use AI to support workers, or mostly to cut costs and reduce headcount? What kind of job do you have, and have you already seen AI start changing your industry? Do you think your role becomes more valuable with AI, or more vulnerable because of it? Five years from now, do you think your job will look mostly the same, or completely different? description: AI is making work more intense and causing mass layoffs. @Michael Mezz
_transcript: A UC Berkeley study has concluded that AI doesn't reduce work. It makes work more intense for the workers using it. Over an eight-month study at a US tech company, researchers found that employees using AI worked at a faster pace, but that didn't lead to more time off. It led to them taking on more work and extending work into more hours of the day. That's because using AI, workers were able to take on responsibilities that had belonged to others. Which sounds great, right? Like more productive workers, what's wrong with that? Well, the issue is that it blurred the boundaries between work and non-work. Employees began using AI to do small amounts of work in time that had previously been breaks, which created a workday with fewer pauses, continual attention switching, and a growing number of open tasks at any given moment. The overall result on workers was more fatigue, more burnout, and a growing sense that work was harder to step away from. So AI does make workers more productive, but at what cost? After all, these productivity gains explain the waves of mass layoffs that we're seeing. And we've seen this before. When automation swept through American factories in the 70s, 80s, and 90s, it didn't free up workers for more opportunities. It just hollowed out entire communities. Detroit, Pittsburgh, Cleveland, they all lost hundreds of thousands of factory jobs as they were automated or shipped overseas. And the wealth from those productivity gains went to the very rich. AI is following that same pattern. So what do we do about it? Well, we need sensible AI policy, like requiring workers to get a say in how AI gets implemented, and a financial safety net for people who get displaced, and bans on the AI-driven wage algorithms that companies are already using to push pay as low as possible. And we need to seriously consider an AI dividend, a direct cash payment to anyone whose creativity is used to train these AI models, which is most of us given that it's trained on the sum of human knowledge. description: A new paper, ‘The AI Layoff Trap,’ from the University of Pennsylvania and Boston University, explores a simple but uncomfortable problem: when companies use AI to cut workers, they may also be cutting the customer demand they depend on.   The problem is not just that workers lose jobs. It is that lost wages can mean less spending across the whole market, so one firm’s layoffs quietly weaken revenue for other firms too. What this paper is trying to do is explain why companies may still keep automating even when that broader outcome is bad for everyone, including business owners. In simple terms, each firm sees its own cost savings clearly, but only feels a small share of the demand damage, because that damage is spread across many competitors. That creates an automation race where the private incentive looks rational, even if the collective result is worse. The idea is that this is not mainly a coordination problem or a lack-of-foresight problem. It is a built-in incentive problem inside competitive markets. The paper’s main takeaway is that helping workers after layoffs may soften the blow, but it does not fully change the incentive to automate too aggressively. Their argument is that only a direct tax on automation, aimed at the demand loss firms impose on everyone else, actually fixes the core distortion.

_transcript: If you have lost your job in the UAE, or you're worried you might, there is a law that was specifically designed to protect you exactly in this situation, and right now is more relevant than ever. The law is called the Involuntary Loss of Employment Scheme, or ILOE for short. It was introduced under Federal Decree Law No. 13 of 2022 and has been mandatory for all private sector and federal government employees since January 2023. The purpose is straightforward. If you lose your job through no fault of your own, the scheme pays you a portion of your salary temporarily while you find your next role. With current regional and geopolitical pressures affecting businesses across several sectors, retail, tourism, logistics, technology, companies are making difficult workforce decisions. This is precisely the scenario the law was designed for, and it works as follows. If you qualify, ILOE pays you 60% of your basic salary for up to 3 months. There are two categories. If your basic salary is AED 16,000 or below, you can receive up to 10,000 dirhams per month. If your salary is about 16,000 dirhams, the cap is 20,000 dirhams per month. This is not insignificant. For many people that covers rent utilities and basic living expenses while they are navigating their transition To be eligible there are several conditions and all of them must be satisfied First you must have been subscribed to the scheme continuously for at least 12 consecutive months, with all premiums paid and up to date. Second, the termination must be involuntary. In other words, you were let go by your employer, not resigned, and not dismissed for disciplinary reasons. Third, your employer must have canceled your work permit before you filed the claim. Fourth, you must have a valid UE residency visa at the time of filing. And fifth, this is the one people miss the most. You must submit your claim within 30 days of the date your employment ends. That deadline is absolute. There are no extensions. Miss it and your claim is automatically rejected, regardless of whether you would have otherwise qualified. The process is handled online through the official ILOE portal or through the ILOE mobile app. You log on in using your Emirates ID, registered mobile number, and submit your claim through the portal. Once submitted and approved, the insurer is required to pay you within two weeks. Payments continue monthly for up to three months or until you find new employment, whichever comes first. In closing, jobs are being lost right now, some of those losses are legitimate, and for the people affected, this scheme exists precisely to provide a bridge. So know your rights and exercise them timely.

description: A lot of the AI conversation focuses on job loss, but MIT economist David Autor has shown that automation works in a more specific way. Technology enters a job and removes certain tasks while leaving others intact. What happens next — higher wages or more competition — depends on whether the hard parts went away or the easy parts did. Follow the series for more on how the story of ai and jobs might play out. #ai #stayhuman #aiandjobs #cognitivesovereignty
_transcript: Taxi drivers and accountants both got automated. One group got poorer, the other got richer. And the reason why is probably the most important idea for understanding what AI is about to do to your job. Before Uber, London cabbies spent years memorising 25,000 streets. It's called the knowledge. That expertise was the entire job. You were paying for what they knew. Then GPS automated the expert part, the hard part, the thing that took years to learn. Suddenly anyone with a car and a phone could do the job. Employment and ride services went up 250%. Wages, flat. Because the hard part was gone and anyone could do what was left. Now look at accountants. Computers automated the routine part, the data entry, the bookkeeping, the repetitive calculations. The easy part, what was left? The complex analytical work, the judgment calls that required more expertise, not less. So wages went up. The job got more specialized and more valuable. Same story. Technology automates part of a job completely opposite outcomes. The difference is whether the technology took the hard parts or the easy parts If the technology takes the hard parts the things that took years to learn the expertise that made you worth paying for you heading towards more competition and lower wages because the barrier to entry just disappeared Machines can come in If the technology takes the easy parts, the routine, the repetitive, the stuff that you didn't need much training for, you're heading towards more specialization and higher wages because now you spend all your time on the work that actually requires you. This is the question you need to be asking right now, Not, will AI take my job? That's the wrong question. The right question is, in my job, is AI taking the hard parts or the easy parts? The tasks that AI could already handle, were those the tasks that took you years to learn, or were they the parts that you could have taught one new hire on day one? because if AI is eating the drudge work and leaving you with the judgment calls, the economics are in your favor. Here’s why they are essential: Storing Everything Every photo you upload, every email you send, and every Netflix show you stream lives on servers in a data centre somewhere. Without them, there would simply be nowhere to store the world's data. Powering the Internet Every website, app, and online service runs on servers. When you search on Google or open Instagram, your request is processed within milliseconds by machines located in data centres, often thousands of kilometres away. Enabling AI This is one of the biggest reasons today. Training and running AI models requires enormous computing power far more than any personal device can handle. Tools like ChatGPT, Google Gemini, and Claude rely on massive clusters of specialised chips such as Nvidia GPUs running 24/7 in data centres. Business Operations Banks, hospitals, governments, and retailers run their core operations including transactions, records, and logistics  on servers hosted either in their own data centres or through cloud providers like AWS, Azure, or Google Cloud. Cloud Computing Services like Google Drive, iCloud, Dropbox, and Microsoft 365 allow you to access your files from any device because your data is not stored on your laptop — it’s stored in a data centre. Resilience and Backup Data centres are built with redundancy. If one server fails, another automatically takes over. They also back up critical data to ensure it is not lost during disasters. The Trade-offs However, data centres also have challenges. They consume large amounts of electricity and water for cooling. A single large facility can use as much power as a small city. This is why the AI boom is creating global discussions about energy infrastructure, nuclear power, and sustainability. Conclusion In short, data centres are to the digital economy what roads, power grids, and warehouses are to the physical economy invisible infrastructure that everything else depends on.

While the concept has been gaining attention as companies look for new ways to power the next wave of AI infrastructure, Huang made it clear that this is not happening anytime soon. He pointed to massive technical and logistical challenges, from launching and maintaining hardware in orbit to ensuring reliable power, cooling, and data transmission back to Earth. description: How much water does it cost to generate one AI image?  Good question, but not necessarily the right one. Instead, today we’re asking WHY data centers need so much water to function, beyond the headlines.  Follow Future in Bloom for more on Solving the AI Power Problem.
_transcript: Data centers don't need to use a lot of water. They do because we chose the laziest cooling design and then scaled it across a trillion-dollar industry. See, AI servers generate a lot of heat. In order to get rid of that heat, most facilities use evaporative cooling. That means that water is sprayed and allowed to evaporate to reduce the heat. A typical hyperscale data center can consume over 200 million gallons of water a year just to cool its equipment. That's the equivalent of a town of tens of thousands of people using water for a year. The better solution is liquid-based cooling, or sometimes called direct-to-chip and immersion cooling. Instead of dumping heat into a room in evaporating water, liquid systems move heat directly off the chip with higher efficiency. Because liquid transfers heat thousands of times more effectively than air, these systems can run in closed loops that dramatically decrease water loss, up to 90% according to industry pilots. To make this mainstream, we need three things. First, design construction defaults that assume liquid cooling for all new builds. Two, we need transparency standards around reporting water use and cooling types publicly. Three, we need policy incentives that treat cooling as infrastructure, not as an afterthought. And if we do this, we don't just get lower water use. We get better performance, lower energy consumption, and most importantly, less community conflict. See, water-intensive data centers aren't a given. they're a design problem we can fix. This is episode five of solving the AI power problem. Follow along to learn more.

_transcript: This is how AI uses water, visually explained. Every time you ask AI a question, that request is sent to a data center and processed by thousands of AI chips. In 2024, data centers used 2% of the world's electricity, but this number is for all data centers that keep the internet running. We don't know what share of that can be attributed to AI alone. It's estimated that a single AI request uses 10 times more energy than a standard search, but this estimate is based on AI models from 2023, which are much smaller than the ones we have today. Second, they need cooling systems to prevent overheating. Most cooling systems use fresh water, and the average data center consumes 300,000 gallons of water every day, which is equivalent to 19,000 showers. Unfortunately, we don't have precise or reliable numbers for how much energy or water AI uses alone because tech companies aren't revealing the size of their newest AI models What we do know is that AI developments and usage are likely to keep increasing over the next few years which will require more data centers aka more electricity and water than before. Thankfully, some solutions are starting to emerge to make AI more energy efficient. And here are three you should know about. First, we could run AI on our personal devices instead of data centers because they've been getting more powerful hardware. This is called edge AI, and we're already seeing signs of it. For example, the new iPhone can run basic AI features on your device directly without sending those requests to a data center. Another solution is called model distillation. The idea is to create smaller models based on large models to make them more energy efficient and cost efficient for specific tasks because we don't always need the biggest and most advanced model if a task is simple. description: Data centers are the backbone of everything online cloud storage, streaming, AI, banking systems, and social media. But behind the screens is a huge physical footprint that many people don’t realize. A single large data center can use 300,000 to over 5 million gallons of water per day just to cool the servers. Some of the biggest facilities use as much water as a town of 30,000–50,000 people, and this demand is rising every year as more companies expand their digital infrastructure. This is where the Great Lakes come into the picture. The Great Lakes hold 20% of the world’s fresh surface water, making the region extremely attractive to corporations looking for reliable, inexpensive, long-term water supplies. While Western states face droughts and restrictions, Michigan and surrounding areas still have large water reserves, cooler temperatures, and lower land costs. To big tech companies, it looks like the perfect place to build. But high water use comes with high consequences. Most data centers cool servers using evaporative cooling, which means the water they take in doesn’t go back to the lake it evaporates into the air and leaves the watershed entirely. Other cooling systems pump water back out, but that water is significantly warmer, contributing to thermal pollution. Warmer water can harm fish populations, disrupt breeding cycles, damage cold-water species, and change lake ecosystems in ways that are hard to reverse. Water used for cooling often contains chemical additives like biocides and anti-corrosion agents. If these aren’t carefully handled, they pose additional environmental risks. Then there’s the energy problem. Data centers use massive power as much electricity as a factory or small city. This increased demand forces utilities to expand infrastructure or build new power sources, often relying on fossil fuels. In many cases, residents end up absorbing these costs through higher energy rates, even though the data center benefits the most. And while companies often promise economic growth, a typical data center only creates 35–100 permanent jobs, far fewer than what local communities expect after offering huge tax breaks. There’s also concern about groundwater. While the Great Lakes appear endless, the aquifers beneath them are not. Heavy industrial water withdrawals, combined with climate change, can lower water tables in surrounding towns and rural communities. Once groundwater levels drop, they may never fully return to normal. Supporters argue that data centers are necessary for economic development, but critics warn that Michigan must proceed cautiously. The Great Lakes Compact protects the basin from excessive water exports, but it does not fully regulate how much water companies can withdraw for industrial use as long as it technically stays within the watershed. Meanwhile, long-term environmental monitoring, public transparency, and community benefits agreements are often minimal. The bottom line: Data centers provide digital convenience, but they come with enormous water and energy costs. With the Great Lakes being one of the most important freshwater systems on Earth, Michigan has a responsibility to ensure these resources aren’t treated as a limitless corporate cooling supply. The lakes belong to the people not private companies looking for cheap water.  #talkaboutit #michigannews #GreatLakes #SustainableLiving #puremichigan

description: The #1 AI implementation skill isn't technical — it's picking the right problem. Most founders automate the wrong thing and wonder why AI didn't save them. Save this before you build your next workflow. #AIImplementation #TheoryOfConstraints #BusinessBottleneck #SmallBusinessAutomation
_transcript: The most important skill set when it comes to implementing AI is not actually your technical knowledge of automation systems or processes. The most important skill is choosing the right problem to fix. It doesn't matter how good of a job you do fixing a problem if it's not the constraint within your business. In manufacturing there's a discipline called the theory of constraints. If you have five bicycle frames, seven handles, and 50 wheels, it doesn't matter how many wheels you've got. You've only got five bicycle frames. You can only make five bikes. Business and other processes work exactly the same way. Your business is a series of systems and processes that all have their own constraints. And it's up to you as the business owner to actually identify what the constraint is of your business and then work on fixing that. It doesn't matter how you fix it and it actually doesn't matter how long it takes you to fix it because working on something else is like making more wheels instead of making more frames. It's not going to help you make more bikes or more money. In my opinion, the way that you do this most effectively is with actually mapping out and modeling the business So you can see here this is an e style business where we got marketing spend along the top row and then that leads to new customer ROAS. From that we've got new customers, repeat customers, we've got cost of goods sold, we've got fulfillment, we've got net profit, contribution profit and then we're actually tracking cash. Now this is just an example but I strongly believe that if you are not tracking this kind of stuff at the top level, then you do not know what direction you are moving in. Creating some kind of sheet like this is actually the foundation of setting up KPIs within your business, because then you can tell, were my predictions correct? They're never correct. But then at least you can see how not correct they were and what you're going to do about it to fix it. And it helps you to identify the bottlenecks. Do you need more traffic? Is your conversion rate down? Are people not coming back and buying again? Is your OPEX too high? Are you paying too much for salaries? There's lots and lots of factors in business that affect your ability to scale and it's up to you to identify which one is the constraint and then aggressively go after that until it is solved and then you can move on to the next one.

description: AI’s energy use already represents as much as 20 percent of global data-center power demand, research published Thursday in the journal Joule shows. That demand from AI, the research states, could double by the end of this year, comprising nearly half of all total data-center electricity consumption worldwide, excluding the electricity used for bitcoin mining. The new research is published in a commentary by Alex de Vries-Gao, the founder of Digiconomist, a research company that evaluates the environmental impact of technology. De Vries-Gao started Digiconomist in the late 2010s to explore the impact of bitcoin mining, another extremely energy-intensive activity, would have on the environment. Looking at AI, he says, has grown more urgent over the past few years because of the widespread adoption of ChatGPT and other large language models that use massive amounts of energy. According to his research, worldwide AI energy demand is now set to surpass demand from bitcoin mining by the end of this year. But there’s still a lot of unknowns about the share that AI, specifically, takes up in that current configuration of electricity use by data centers. Data centers power a variety of services—like hosting cloud services and providing online infrastructure—that aren’t necessarily linked to the energy-intensive activities of AI. description: Impact of AI on our oceans 🌊🐠🐧 #ai #datacenter #ocean #climate #climatechange
_transcript: Hi guys, there's something I wanted to share with you, and it's funny I'm using social media to share that, but at first there seemed to be no connection between chatting with the AI, posting a video, or scrolling on social media, and the rising temperatures of our oceans. The global data infrastructure that powers our online lives consumes vast amounts of water, electricity, and resources. These choices ripple outward, ultimately shaping the health of our oceans and the climate they stabilize. Data centers hold their social media feed, train AI models, deliver endless streams of video. In 2024, they consumed 415 terawatt hours, and experts project that those numbers are only going to rise and double by 2030. For an average of 945 TWh? Much of electricity comes from fossil fuels and carbon dioxide released when oil, gas and coal are burned does not vanish. It accumulates in the atmosphere, trapping heat. Over 90 of this is absorbed by the oceans As a result the more of our digital appetite grows the more the sea is warm The impacts are not limited to energy Data centers must stay cool, and many of them rely on water for that purpose. A single facility can use millions of gallons each day, turning it to rivers and oceans at much higher temperature. Globally, data centers are responsible for 560 billion liters of water used every year. That number is only going to double by 2030. Warmer water released into a local ecosystem disrupts fish population, coral reefs, and alters the natural balance of aquatic life. The oceans, once a stabilizing force, become more fragile under that pressure. AI adds another layer. AI accounts for roughly 20% of data centers electricity use, and the numbers are only going to climb. Training a single model utilizes as much electricity as a small city does in several months. What feels like an invisible, weightless activity, generating a picture asking AI model scrolling endless feed is a part of immense and resource hungry system The consequences are not abstract Warmer oceans only accelerate the melting of ice in Antarctica and Greenland pushing the sea levels higher. They fuel stronger hurricanes by adding more energy to storms. They drive mass coral bleaching events and shift the migration patterns of fish populations. The oceans regulate our climate, our weather, our food systems. the very stability of coastal communities. When it warms, the entire Earth system changes. But there are real choices on industry level and on personal level. Data centers beginning to shift towards renewable energy, invest in innovating cooling systems, design systems that reuse waste heat or locate near hydropower. These efforts matter, but they're not enough on their own. Personal responsibility plays a role too. Every scroll, every video, every AI prompt, and reducing that weight begins with a mindful use. Doom scrolling, endlessly consuming negative content, not only harms mental health, it fuels the cycle of digital demand Choosing to pause before clicking next reducing redundant AI requests deleting unused files and opting for greener platforms are small acts that collectively reduce the burden of our shared infrastructure. These are acts of self-care that also ripple outward into planetary care. Hidden link between our phones and the oceans reminds us that technology is never immaterial. It is grounded in wires, servers, energy, and water. The oceans absorb the vast majority of the warming we already caused. They cannot do so endlessly. The arising heat is a warning, one that asks us to rethink how we live, consume, and connect. Next time you find yourself doomscrolling or deciding what to do next, pause and remember every click is connected to our climate and every pause is a step toward balance but being mindful of our digital choices lighten the load we place on the seas and we reclaim the responsibility for the world that our technology is shaping i love you until next time bye

_transcript: Google veut révolutionner les prévisions météo. Le géant vient de présenter dans la revue Nature son nouveau programme basé sur l'IA, son nom Gencast. Concrètement, Gencast serait capable de fournir des prévisions quotidiennes et d'anticiper des situations extrêmes jusqu'à 15 jours à l'avance. Aujourd'hui, il faut savoir que la référence mondiale, c'est le modèle européen ENS. Les deux modèles ont été mis en compétition sur 1320 désastres climatiques en 2019. Et selon les chercheurs de Google, Gencast a formulé de meilleures prévisions dans 97% des cas. Sur les tempêtes tropicales, par exemple, le modèle de Google aurait pu prévenir en moyenne 12 heures plus tôt. Sur sa rapidité, Gencast a analysé des données de 1979 à 2018 avec des variables, la température, la vitesse du vent et la pression atmosphérique. Il peut produire des prévisions de l'évolution du temps sur 15 jours en seulement 8 minutes, contre plusieurs heures aujourd'hui. Par exemple, ces prévisions sur le typhon Ajibi qui avait ravagé le Japon en 2019. Le modèle montre des trajectoires variées qui se précisent de plus en plus à mesure que le cyclone approche. Gencast ne va pas remplacer les modèles actuels puisque l'IA a besoin d'être nourri de données actualisées. Les météorologues sont aussi très prudents, ils préfèrent s'appuyer sur la simulation physique plus rigoureuse. Le modèle va être en open source et la prochaine étape va être de publier des prévisions en temps réel.

description: When you hear the word “AI,” what comes to mind? For most people, it’s chatbots, deepfakes, and maybe a sci-fi image of humanoid robots. But beyond the hype and headlines, there’s a quieter, more powerful shift happening—AI is being used as a real-world climate solution. AI Drones Bringing Dead Forests Back to Life Take Brazil, for example. In a country devastated by deforestation and wildfires, one of these startups is deploying AI-guided drones to replant forests in places humans simply can’t reach. Here’s how it works: drones equipped with cameras and sensors map damaged areas, while AI algorithms analyze the terrain to determine the exact best locations for seeds to take root. Then, the drones drop thousands of seeds per day—faster, cheaper, and more accurately than manual reforestation crews ever could. This approach doesn’t just plant trees; it restores entire ecosystems. It creates habitats for wildlife, helps regulate local climates, and pulls carbon dioxide from the air—slowing the pace of climate change in one of the most critical regions on Earth. Imagine a swarm of drones silently flying over a scarred forest, leaving behind the beginnings of a vibrant green canopy. It’s like a digital lifeline for nature. Stopping Wildfires Before They Spread Meanwhile in Canada, another startup is tackling one of the most destructive consequences of climate change—wildfires. Their system combines AI, satellites, and ground sensors to detect tiny warning signs long before a blaze becomes uncontrollable. It looks for subtle patterns: unusual heat pockets, changes in wind speed, vegetation dryness, or even small smoke signatures invisible to the human eye. When the AI predicts danger, it sends early alerts to local authorities, giving firefighters a critical window of time to act. Preventing one massive wildfire not only saves lives and homes but also keeps millions of tons of carbon from being released into the atmosphere. This is AI as an early warning system for the planet—technology literally buying us time against a warming world. Beyond Trees and Fires: Clean Water, Biodiversity & Carbon Markets Other startups in the program are pushing AI into areas we don’t always think about when we talk about climate:     •    Monitoring water quality in rivers and lakes in real-time, detecting pollution instantly before it spreads.     •    Tracking endangered species and mapping out critical habitats to protect biodiversity.     •    Helping indigenous communities participate in carbon markets, using AI and blockchain to measure and verify the environmental impact of their conservation work—allowing them to benefit financially while protecting their land. This is the kind of innovation that aligns tech with local communities and ecosystems, rather than exploiting them. And this isn’t just feel-good PR. Independent research backs it up. A study led by economist Nicholas Stern estimates that AI could cut between 3.2 to 5.4 billion tons of global emissions every year by 2035. That’s the equivalent of removing up to a quarter of emissions from energy, transport, and food sectors combined—and it still stays net-positive even after accounting for AI’s own energy needs. What makes this different from so many other AI headlines is intentionality. These startups aren’t trying to replace humans or chase the next viral trend—they’re using AI as a tool for climate resilience, restoration, and prevention. It’s a shift in perspective: AI doesn’t have to be a threat to nature; it can be its ally. From tiny rainforest seedlings to intelligent wildfire sensors, these projects are showing us what happens when innovation meets environmental stewardship. If this gives you hope for what’s possible, share this story—because Tech x Nature = Hope. #AI #ClimateTech #Sustainability #GreenTech #AIForGood #PlanetPositive #Innovation #FutureOfTech

_transcript: From your smartphone to algorithms on Netflix and Amazon, artificial intelligence is becoming part of daily life. And now, AI is being used for your daily weather forecasts. Environment and Climate Change Canada recently announced it will use artificial intelligence in its weather forecasts beginning this spring. The department is launching a new hybrid model, part AI and part traditional physics-based model, which will be better able to predict major systems like winter storms, heat waves, and atmospheric rivers. While ECC is using the hybrid approach, other government weather agencies and private companies have jumped in with their own dedicated AI models. The European Centre for Medium-Range Forecasts launched its artificial intelligence forecasting system in early 2025. And for some variables, such as near-surface temperatures and mid-level atmospheric conditions, it's outperforming the traditional physics-based model by up to 20%. Meanwhile, Google's GraphCast can generate a highly accurate 10-day global forecast in under one minute. By using decades of historical weather data, these AI-driven models can make huge improvements to the forecast. But they do have their limits, especially with local variables like wind speeds near specific mountain ranges. While the advancements in forecast accuracy are a great step, we still have a long way to go. I use at least a dozen different forecast models right now, and I see on a daily basis just how different the projections can be, whether it's predicting the track of an incoming storm or timing out how quickly the low-level clouds and fog will retreat back to the coast in the early summer. At the end of the day, predicting the future is tough when you have as many moving variables as the atmosphere does, especially here in the Maritimes. Ryan Snodden, CBC News, Halifax. Thank you.

_transcript: Artificial intelligence is making your electricity worse. You might not have even known that that was a possibility, for your power to be good or bad. We typically experience electricity in a binary sense of available or not, but it can be judged in a qualitative sense as well. And the electricity near AI data centers? Well, it's bad. This is what your power is supposed to look like, at least in North America—a 60 Hz sine wave. AI, however, is causing it to look a bit more like this. These are harmonic distortions—deviations from perfection. Now, power is never perfect. There's always some harmonic distortion, but there's a threshold that is considered acceptable—8%, and when a household is near a major data center cluster, research has indicated that the likelihood that readings exceed that threshold goes dramatically up. This has implications. Your refrigerator, for example, includes a motor to operate its compressor. When the current is not smooth, the fluctuations in power will lead to fluctuations in torque as it spins around its axis, meaning, in addition to the rotational force it's intended to create, it'll also create oscillations as it spins. As these oscillations interact with the motor casing and surrounding components, it creates noise, a rattling sound. So that's to say, AI is making your refrigerator louder. And that noise is more than just annoying. It's representative of mechanical stress that will lead that motor to die out sooner, spoiling your groceries and mandating a costly cumbersome fix The same applies to all the rest of your electronics The 8 harmonic distortion threshold is set since it what normal household appliances can handle without shortening their lifespans so incrementally and ever so slightly, AI is costing you money by making your electronics wear down faster. It's no secret that artificial intelligence, in its current form, is tremendously energy-intensive. That undoubtedly matters, but demand is potentially the simpler problem to solve, especially when ignoring carbon goals. The issue is not just how much power AI uses, it's how and where it uses it. Making AI a net positive for everyday Americans, in particular, considering the tech sector's concentration in the country, will be an enormous challenge not just due to the potential implications on employment and creativity and disinformation and more, but also just due to the sheer strain on the electric grid. Now, data centers, the generic kind, are really nothing new. Take Google, for instance. They opened this one in 2003, this one in 2007, and this one in 2009, just to name a few. From harboring personal emails and documents saved to Google's cloud to powering Google maps or hosting third-party virtual machines or apps, it's this network of brick-and-mortar data centers that's providing the physical infrastructure for Google to become a one-stop shop for all things cloud computing for decades now. And like a simple Google search or Gmail response relies on these data centers so too does an AI query Where the difference lies between a cloud computing data center and an AI data center is in the chips processing units at the heart of them In the middle of 2024, the title of world's most valuable public company belonged not to Microsoft or Apple, but to NVIDIA, a company historically recognized and associated with its ties to video game development. From a $400 billion market cap to $3 trillion in a couple of years, the astronomical rise of NVIDIA was largely attributable to what they're able to supply for AI data centers, the H100 GPU chip. GPUs, or Graphic Processing Units, are what make AI possible. At the simplest level, these chips are capable of working through all the tasks laid out by AI at the same time through parallel processing. Meaning, their thousands of cores, each effectively a tiny calculator, can solve thousands of equations at the exact same time. Tasks that a core processing unit just can't do at the same scale. If a CPU, which is what you'll typically find running the show within a data center, is an electric car capable of taking care of one process extremely quickly and efficiently, then a GPU is a semi-truck, getting a whole lot of tasks done at once, but taking a good bit of gas to do it. Powering such semi-trucks like Nvidia's H100 takes a lot of energy. At peak power consumption, an H100 consumes 700 watts, not far off from a small household appliance like an air fryer. But when run at 61% annual utilization for an entire year, this consumption starts to creep up to about the consumption of a typical American household. Take the total amount of compute required to train a current AI model. This is measured in flops, floating-point operations per second, or really, petaflops, which is one quadrillion flops. This is a graph of required compute per model. Consider the y-axis that makes this possible to even plot. The growth is exponential. GPT-1, for instance, required 18,000 petaflops, while GPT-4 required some 21 billion. description: How do you bring a century-old power grid into the digital age? ⚡️💻 You need a universal language. Meet IEC 61850. For decades, electrical substations were a mess of thousands of copper wires connecting every single device. It was expensive, heavy, and hard to change. As this infographic shows, IEC 61850 changes everything by digitizing the entire substation stack: 1️⃣ The Process Bus (Orange Line): Instead of analog copper wires, "Merging Units" down at the equipment level convert signals into digital data streams (SMV) sent over fiber optics. 2️⃣ The Speed (Right Panel): It uses super-fast peer-to-peer messages called GOOSE to trip circuit breakers instantly when something goes wrong—faster than a human could blink. 3️⃣ The Interoperability (Left Panel): Because it uses "Abstract Data Models," devices from different manufacturers (like Siemens, GE, or ABB) can finally understand each other without custom translators. It’s the global standard that is making the Smart Grid possible. 🌍🔋 #IEC61850 #SmartGrid #PowerEngineering #SubstationAutomation #ElectricalEngineering

Around the 2010s I started realizing that copyright abolition needs to go hand in hand with greater protection of personal information. Social media companies like Facebook rose to monopoly status by two means. Owning the exclusive rights to the code on which the platform is built and tracking our personal information. description: Artists are fighting back against AI #animation #artist #noai #humanartist #tiktokpartner
_transcript: Artists are fighting back against Twitter's AI, and the way they're doing it is absolute genius. It all started when the platform introduced a new feature that very quickly became controversial, that of course being the edit image button. It was a button that was directly baked into every post containing an image on the platform, and allowed anybody to alter the image just by clicking it using AI. Obviously, this upset a lot of artists on the platform, because it literally allowed anybody with one click to alter their artwork with AI. However, artists very quickly realized how to beat the system. See, the edit image button actually only showed up on photo posts, so if you posted your art in a different type of file, like say a GIF, it actually wouldn't have the option to modify it with AI. And so the entirety of the artist community on Twitter unified and entered a renaissance of making GIFs. Some people genuinely made little cute animations that fit the gif format, and some people just exported their static images as gifs. What this also led to, though, was an era of jump scares getting hidden in artwork. Because people were getting conditioned to assume that static artwork was getting exported as gifs, but was still static artwork. And it was a lie. It was not static artwork. Twitter's AI stuff is always such a mess, but you can also always count on artists to find creative ways around it.

description: no tengo nada interesante que decir al respecto así que  Para entender la historia de Five Nights at Freddy's hay que olvidarse que estos son juegos y quiero que tomen realmente a esta saga como lo que es. ¿Terror? Sí, pero sobre todo, ciencia ficción. Antes de comenzar, quiero decir que esta cronología la realizamos entre 3 youtubers conocidos de Five Nights at Freddy's y yo. Por lo tanto, agradecería que si les gusta el contenido de este juego vayan a visitar sus canales. Ahora sí, empecemos. ¿Qué pasaría si dos amigos se abren una pizzería? Esa es la primera pregunta que hay que plantearnos. Lo normal sería que todo vaya medianamente bien con algún tipo de problemas, pero nada saldría más allá de eso. La pregunta cambia completamente si nos preguntamos ¿Qué pasaría si Henry y William abren una pizzería? ¿Quiénes son estos personajes? En un principio, grandes amigos. Henry, por un lado, era un ferviente y talentoso mecánico que cuidaba a su única hija, Charlie. No sabemos nada de su esposa, ni siquiera si tiene a alguien más en su familia. Y por el otro lado, William Afton. La familia de Afton estaba compuesta por 5 miembros. William, una persona con mucho dinero y con buena capacidad para la mecánica. Su hija menor, Elizabeth. Este pendejo que no sabemos el nombre, pero llora todo el tiempo, así que vamos a ponerle Crying Child. Michael Afton, su hijo mayor y su esposa, de quien no se sabe nada. Estos dos personajes unieron sus capacidades de mecánicos y con el buen capital que tenía William ahorrado, entre los dos abrieron un restaurante. Así fue como entre los años 1980 a 1982, supuestamente, Fredbear Family Dinner abrió sus puertas. La principal atracción de este lugar eran los animatrónicos. ¿Qué son? Bueno, básicamente eran robots que podrían ser controlados tanto por ellos mismos como por personas o por almas. Estos animatrónicos habían sido desarrollados por los dueños del restaurante, pero Henry destacó un poco más debido a que hizo un complejo sistema de resortes que permitía a la persona usar estos trajes. Solamente que tenía que ser extremadamente cuidadosa, ya que de lo contrario el mecanismo del mismo se activaría y la persona que esté dentro seguramente quedaría lastimada. Estos trajes híbridos darían a luz en un principio a su principal éxito, Fredbear y Spring Bonnie. Dos animatrónicos que durante esos años 80s habían hecho furor y tan bien les estaba yendo a estos dos amigos que la competencia empezó a llegar. Y es por eso que a unos pocos meses de la salida de Fredbear Family Dinner llegaría su competencia, Fazbear Entertainment, pero que esta no sería relevante hasta en un futuro. En paralelo a estos hechos, empezaban a haber roces entre la dupla principal, ya que William no solamente había abierto el restaurante para comer, sino que detrás de sus intenciones había algo mucho más oscuro, matar gente. Es por eso que en una fecha que desconocemos, William creó un nuevo local, Circus Baby Pizza World, y es en este donde presentaría sus nuevos animatrónicos, los Funtime. Estos animatrónicos estarían hechos bajo la empresa Afton Robotics, que como podrán imaginar, esta empresa era de William. Aunque los Funtime no eran animatrónicos normales, si bien tenían características muy innovadoras con respecto a los primeros trajes híbridos, estos Funtime estarían creados específicamente para matar. Una inteligencia artificial muy avanzada, poder abrir diferentes partes de su cuerpo y la posibilidad de hablar. Claramente no tenían una buena intención, pero a William se le volvería todo en contra cuando el mismo día de la inauguración de su local, a pesar de sus advertencias a Elizabeth, esta entró igual al cuarto donde estaban los animatrónicos para ver si estaba su robot favorito, Baby. Y luego de que este animatrónico le ofreciera un helado para hacer que se acercara a ella, la mata.

_transcript: AI art officially can't be copyrighted in the US. The Supreme Court recently declined to hear Thaler v. Paramutter, a case where computer scientist Stephen Thaler tried to copyright an image that his AI system Dabbas made back in 2012. The catch was that he listed the AI as the author and not himself. Every court has now ruled against him, and by refusing to hear this case, the Supreme Court effectively cements that human authorship is a bedrock requirement when it comes to copyright. Even the Trump administration urged them not to take the case. This has pretty big implications. If you're using AI to generate character, artwork, or other creative assets without meaningful human contribution, that work could essentially belong in the public domain. So then anyone could use it and then you have no legal standing to stop them. The ruling also follows Thayer's failed patent case where he tried to list Dabbas as an inventor. Same result there. The patent office said that only natural persons can be listed as inventors. Fowler called the decision substrate chauvinism. Basically, the assumption that creativity must come from a biological brain. But legal experts do point out that this case doesn't actually cover human AI collaborations, just fully autonomous AI creations. The real question now is whether Congress or other entities will step in to clarify the rules. So far, they haven't really said anything. Follow for Tech and AI News.

Como habrás oído, este informe lo van entregando por partes. La primera parte aborda el tema de las réplicas digitales, o sea, el uso de tecnología digital para copiar de forma realista la voz o apariencia de una persona. La segunda parte era muy esperada porque entrega alineamientos sobre si es que la obra creada con Inteligencia Artificial puede ser protegida por copyright. ¿Qué significa esto? Que alguien pueda reclamar su propiedad o autoría, incluso darle uso comercial. Incluso algunos se frotaban las manos diciendo ya no tengo que pagar a un artista y puedo generar esa obra yo mismo. Y bueno, a continuación te resumo las principales conclusiones para que estés enterado antes de usar obra generada con inteligencia artificial y por qué es tan importante el precedente que sienta este informe. Primero, la autoría humana es el requisito fundamental para que exista protección o copyright en obras generadas por IA. Segundo, el copyright para obras generadas por IA puede estar justificado en los siguientes escenarios. Uso de IA como apoyo. Las obras producidas con asistencia de herramientas IA pueden tener copyright siempre que el resultado implique suficiente creatividad humana. Importante, los prompts por sí solos no satisfacen ese umbral de creatividad humana. Input y output expresivo. Contenido creativo de autoría humana modificado por IA puede tener copyright limitado solo a la parte hecha por humanos. Obras derivadas de aquellas generadas por IA pueden tener copyright solo en la porción que tenga autoría humana. Selección y organización. La selección, organización y ordenación de material generado por IA que demuestre originalidad y creatividad puede tener copyright limitado únicamente a la selección, organización y ordenación realizados por autores humanos. Los prompts por sí solos no bastan para obtener copyright en obras generadas por IA. La USCO las ve como simples instrucciones que no generan resultados predecibles. _transcript: The images that you see here are created by artificial intelligence by a software called Midjourney. And the author of the comic book called Zarya of the Dead submitted the book to the Copyright Office for registration and got a detailed response back. Now this response is regard to registration of this particular comic book, but it serves as a great roadblock for anybody using AI generated material in their works. So we start with the general position of the Copyright Office, which is that AI-generated works is not protected by copyright because copyright requires a human author. So these images aren't subject to copyright protection, even though she created the prompts that led to those images being generated. Second, this text. That's her own text, and that's original to her, and that's sufficiently creative. So the text of the comic book is protected by copyright, which means she can register the copyright in the comic book. She has to disclaim the images generated by AI because those images are essentially public domain. Next is the compilation copyright. Lastly, there's her enhancement of the images, her editing of the images for which she used Photoshop, as you can see here. The Copyright Office says that's not sufficiently original to be protected by copyright. Now, editing images that are in the public domain can sometimes be protected by copyright, but what you see here is not. So if you look at all that, you get your roadmap to what's protected by copyright and what's not, at least in this instance. And you can look up this letter in the Copyright Office database. description: Meta’s copyright battle with a group of authors, including Sarah Silverman and Ta-Nehisi Coates, will turn on the question of whether the company’s AI tools produce works that can cannibalize the authors’ book sales. US District Court Judge Vince Chhabria spent several hours grilling lawyers from both sides after they each filed motions for partial summary judgement, meaning they want Chhabria to rule on specific issues of the case rather than leaving each one to be decided at trial. The authors allege that Meta illegally used their work to build its generative AI tools, emphasizing that the company pirated their books through “shadow libraries” like LibGen. The social media giant is not denying that it used the work or that it downloaded books from shadow libraries en masse, but insists that its behavior is shielded by the “fair use” doctrine, an exception in US copyright law that allows for permissionless use of copyrighted work in certain cases, including parody, teaching, and news reporting. If Chhabria grants either motion, he’ll issue a ruling before the case goes to trial—and likely set an important precedent shaping how courts deal with generative AI copyright cases moving forward. Kadrey v. Meta is one of the dozens of lawsuits filed against AI companies that are currently winding through the US legal system.

description: A team of computer scientists at the University of Chicago, led by Professor Ben Zhao, built a tool called Nightshade. It allows artists to add invisible perturbations to their images before uploading them online. To the human eye, nothing changes. But if those images are scraped into an AI training set, the model mislearns. Dogs become cats. Cars become cows. Outputs degrade. It was downloaded over 250,000 times in its first five days. The goal, as the researchers stated, was not to destroy AI. It was to make training on unlicensed work so unreliable and costly that paying artists becomes the rational economic choice. This is asymmetric resistance. One artist poisoning images does nothing. A hundred thousand doing it changes the cost structure of training. AI companies have responded by developing filtering techniques to detect and remove poisoned data, and by investing in licensed datasets and synthetic data generation. The arms race between poisoning tools and detection tools is ongoing, and neither side has a decisive advantage. #AI #ArtificialIntelligence #AIGovernance #DataCenters #FutureOfWork

_transcript: As an artist myself, who's been drawing my entire life and who plans to continue drawing for the rest of my life, I wanted to give my own current thoughts on the whole AI art controversy. It's no news to anybody that AI has been making leaps and bounds with ChatGPT, CactusAI, and of course the notorious MidJourney Art Generator. As an artist, I've heard other artists talking about it, and the main controversy lies in this idea of A, replacing artists, and B, plagiarism from the AI. I've heard a lot of artists saying that Mid Journey and other art simulators are plagiarizing from other artists and using that as a justification for why it's bad and should be canceled. Whereas that does have some merit, I feel like the crux of the issue is not that at all. Because when I think about this objectively, all the AI is doing is referencing art from all over the internet based on a prompt to generate a new image. And that's not unlike what the human brain does, right? When I wanted to make a piece of art, I looked at a bunch of images that are similar to what I'm thinking of and used those and draw elements from the different various pieces of artwork to create my own artwork. And that's how people even develop their own art styles. They look at artists they like, they take elements that they like, and put it together. So as the AI is doing essentially what the human brain does it seems a little bit off target or a little bit ridiculous to say that AI is stealing from artists but artists aren stealing from artists when they do the same thing But if you ask me I think the real concern about AI art is about phasing artists out of the artistic process On simpler terms, artists aren't going to be able to charge a lot of money for art pieces that people can just generate with AI. But I think that too is also a ridiculous claim, because at the end of the day, art is and has always been a mode of self-expression, expressing yourself through your medium. It's about communicating ideas, emotions, and themes that are so complex that they can't be said that you communicate through artwork. And obviously, AI just being a machine or a tool is completely incapable of doing that, as this is inherent to the human experience. So I think the real concern for a lot of artists, which is a valid concern, is that they can't charge, let's say, $500 for a commission anymore if somebody can just generate it with AI. But my problem with that is by looking at it in that way, all you're doing is causing the problem in which you're complaining about. What do I mean by that? The problem is if you're turning a mode of self-expression into a consumer utility, you're essentially being your own worst enemy. Because as part of the capitalistic consumerist market, the goal is to make things as simple as possible, which inevitably phases humans out and replaces them with robots. And we see this at your local CVS where self-checkout is replaced by humans. So at the end of the day, the artistic process is not going to be destroyed because of Art AI in the same way that ChatGPT isn't going to ruin writing for authors. Rather, it's going to reframe the relationship between capitalism and art.

Police say AI-driven facial recognition helped identify a Tennessee woman as a “potential suspect” in a North Dakota fraud case, though she claims she’s never been to North Dakota. She spent months in jail before charges were dismissed. Police have since acknowledged errors in the investigation.
_transcript: This woman was arrested in Tennessee for alleged fraud in North Dakota. But here's the thing, she says she's never even been there. Police say AI-driven facial recognition technology helped identify her as a potential suspect. We're happy to acknowledge when we make errors and we've made a few in this case for sure. Angela Lips, a 50-year-old grandmother, was arrested in July on a warrant tied to bank fraud cases in Fargo, North Dakota, according to police. Fargo police chief Dave Zabulski told CNN that investigators used facial recognition from a partner agency, as well as other investigative steps, quote, independent from AI. That system, used by West Fargo police, flagged lips as a potential suspect based on an image from a fake ID used in the fraud case, Zabulski said at a news conference. Our partner agency over at West Fargo purchased their own AI facial recognition system that we were not aware of at the executive level anyway. We would not have allowed that to be used and it has since been prohibited. West Fargo police shared the report from the AI tool with Fargo police, though it didn't have enough evidence to charge anyone and only shared information, the department said in a statement. Lips lawyers say bank records later showed she was in Tennessee at the time of the alleged crimes. She spent more than three months in a Tennessee jail before being extradited to North Dakota, according to Fargo police and her lawyers. Lips described her extradition in a GoFundMe page launched to help her rebuild her life, writing that she was terrified and exhausted and humiliated. In December, prosecutors moved to dismiss the charges after informing police that the defense produced, quote, potential expulatory evidence. Lips was released on Christmas Eve. Police have not issued an apology, saying the case is still ongoing and charges could be refiled. Zabulski added, police are still considering any disciplinary measures for officers involved in the investigation. The case comes as police departments across the US expand their use of AI tools, even as experts warned they could lead to serious mistakes if not carefully verified. LIPS lawyers say they're now exploring civil rights claims.

description: The government has announced the rollout of 40 new live facial recognition vans, supported by artificial intelligence, as part of what it calls sweeping policing reforms. Live facial recognition is not a passive camera system. It captures faces in real time, converts them into biometric identifiers, and compares them against watchlists using probabilistic matching. This process inherently carries error rates, bias risks, and data retention questions. Once mobile, this capability moves beyond fixed locations and targeted deployments. It becomes adaptable, scalable, and harder for the public to observe or challenge. Oversight mechanisms often lag behind deployment, and legal safeguards are tested after the technology is already in use. The core issue is not whether technology can assist policing. It is whether democratic controls, transparency, and accountability expand at the same pace as surveillance capability. History suggests they rarely do. #FacialRecognition #Surveillance #CivilLiberties #Policing #Technology Mobile biometric surveillance increases reach and frequency Accuracy and bias remain unresolved technical risks Public consent is unclear in live deployments Oversight often follows deployment, not precedes it Power concentrates when systems scale faster than scrutiny

_transcript: Facial recognition software might seem like magic, but it's all about complex algorithms and patterns. Here's how it works in a nutshell. First, the software captures an image of a face using cameras or existing photos. This image isn't just stored as is. The system analyzes key features like the distance between your eyes, the shape of your nose, or the contours of your jawline. These measurements create a unique facial signature. Next, this facial signature is compared to a database of known faces. This database could be for unlocking your phone, identifying you at an airport, or even tagging you in photos. The software uses machine learning to improve accuracy. This means it learns from millions of images to get better at recognizing people over time. But is it perfect? Not quite. Variations in lighting, angles, or even identical twins can confuse the system. Plus, privacy concerns make facial recognition a hot topic for debate. So whether you're unlocking a device or walking through an airport, facial recognition software is using science and data to make quick decisions. description: This post from Liberty highlights a deeply concerning issue surrounding the unchecked use of live facial recognition (LFR) technology by police in the UK, specifically the Metropolitan Police. A man was wrongly flagged by the system and mistaken for a wanted person — a stark reminder of the real-world harm caused by flawed or unregulated technology. He describes the experience as “stop and search on steroids”, underscoring how LFR compounds existing issues of over-policing and racial profiling. Liberty is calling for urgent legislative safeguards to rein in this powerful surveillance tool. According to the second image, their key demands include: 	•	Independent sign-off before LFR can be used. 	•	Strict limits on when it can be deployed — only for: 	•	Finding missing persons or victims of serious crimes like trafficking or exploitation. 	•	Preventing imminent threats to life or safety. 	•	Locating suspects in serious criminal cases. 	•	Ensuring watchlists only include images directly relevant to those purposes. 	•	Providing the public with at least 14 days’ notice before LFR is used. The overarching message: Without clear legal restrictions, live facial recognition threatens civil liberties, fosters discriminatory practices, and risks irreversible harm to innocent people. Liberty and other campaigners demand transparency, accountability, and meaningful regulation — or better yet, a complete ban on police use of the technology in public spaces. This is more than a privacy issue — it’s about power, discrimination, and justice in the digital age. description: One overlooked ADHD experience is the discomfort some people feel with silence. For some, background stimulation—music, television, podcasts, ambient noise—can function less as distraction and more as regulation. When external stimulation drops, internal cognitive activity may become more noticeable, including racing thoughts, unfinished tasks, self-criticism, or emotional overwhelm. What may look like “always needing noise” can sometimes be the nervous system attempting to manage internal intensity. Understanding this can reduce shame and help reframe certain behaviors as adaptive strategies rather than flaws. ⚠️ This content is for educational and informational purposes only and reflects general clinical insight. It is not medical advice, mental health advice, or a substitute for professional evaluation, diagnosis, or treatment. Viewing this content does not establish a therapeutic relationship. Individual experiences may vary. Please consult a qualified professional for personalized support. Dr. Joseph Pagano, DSW, LCSW, ADHD-CCSP, C-PD practices in Pennsylvania and West Virginia, with California coming soon. _transcript: People think ADHD means you can't sit still, but here's what they miss. Sometimes it's not movement you can tolerate. _transcript: There's three main styles of facial recognition. The first one is facial identification. The second application is face verification. And the third sort of form of facial recognition is this idea of facial analysis. Identification is one-to-many matching. The software takes one face and compares it to a large database of faces to determine the unknown person's identity. Verification, on the other hand, is one-to-one matching. It's used to confirm a person is who they say they are, like when I use my face to unlock my phone. The new image of my face is compared to a known image that's already stored. Then there's facial analysis, which looks at gender, age, race. It's even sometimes used to try to predict how I'm feeling by the expression on my face.

description: What does facial recognition actually ‘see’ when it scans your face? Here are some of the things it’s looking for to make a match. #facialrecognition #privacy #technology
_transcript: What does facial recognition technology see? First, it finds a face in the picture. It ignores the rest of the scene and just focuses on the face. Next, it maps key points that are unique to your face, like the distance between your eyes, the shape of your jaw, and where your nose and mouth sit. Think of it as a dot-to-dot pattern, which is then turned into your unique face print or a code. It then compares that code to find a match, or to check you are who you say you are. Some systems even use things like skin texture patterns, ear shape, hairline outline, 3D depth info, and infrared patterns.

description: Social media users are sharing AI-generated images, claiming that they’re from security camera footage of Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. #TheCube explains why these claims are false and completely unfounded.
_transcript: Social media users are sharing these AI-generated images, falsely claiming that they're from security camera footage of Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky with convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. In the pictures, we can see a figure resembling Zelensky shaking hands and talking with Epstein, with the captions alleging that the two were close and met each other in intimate, non-public settings on the disgraced financier's private island. However, there's plenty of evidence to prove that the images are fake. Firstly, we ran them through Google's AI platform Gemini, which detected a synth ID on the image. This is an invisible watermark developed by Google, which shows that all or part of the content was created or modified using Google's AI tools. The images are also grainy and low quality, which is typical of AI-generated content that tries to hide inconsistencies and mimic security camera footage. Additionally, the timeline doesn't add up. The picture shows Zelensky as he has appeared since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in early 2022. But Epstein died in August 2019, only a few months after Zelensky became president. There's no credible evidence that the two ever met. The Cube has trawled through the Epstein files, the latest tranche of which was released in January. And while Zelensky's name does appear in them, it's only in the context of news reports or the 2019 elections that saw him become president. This isn't the first time that false claims have tried to link Zelensky and Epstein. Other fact-checkers have debunked previous instances where pro-Russian Telegram channels spread false narratives of a connection between Zelensky, Epstein and human trafficking. Following the release of the latest files, other European politicians were falsely labelled as having links to Epstein, including France's President Emmanuel Macron and the leader of the British far-right party Reform UK, Nigel Farage. _transcript: New AI cameras that can catch drivers breaking the law are being rolled out from today, with artificial intelligence able to capture six separate driver offenses. It's claimed that the AI cameras can capture drivers speeding, using their phone while driving, failing to wear a seatbelt, failing to stop at a red light, driving without a valid MOT, and driving without insurance. The software works by capturing footage of passing vehicles, which is then run through AI. Two precise photos are taken, one taken at an angle that captures as whether or not the driver has a phone to their ear and if their seatbelt is being worn, the second is taken from a deeper angle which can capture if the driver is messaging on their device. The software is capable of capturing images during the day or at night in almost any weather conditions. The state of the art cameras are set to be deployed in the Greater Manchester area from September 3rd as part of a wider national trial. Greater Manchester isn't the first UK region to try out the tech as a similar trial in Cornwall last year saw 300 Brits caught out within just three days.

description: “Meta tracks your eyes through your phone’s infrared camera.” This myth is circulating again. Let’s kill it. The claim: Your phone’s Face ID uses infrared to scan your face. It tracks where your eyes are looking. Meta has access to it. So when you scroll, they know exactly what you look at. Sounds scary. Also completely false. Apps like Instagram, Facebook, TikTok can’t use it. Period. What Meta actually tracks: They don’t need eye tracking. They use behavioral data. What matters: * Watch time (retention) * Rewatches * Likes, comments, shares * Clicks (CTR) * Scroll stops (dwell time) * Searches * Follows * Saves This tells them far more than eye tracking ever could. Why the myth feels real: You see a hiking ad. Then another. Then another. Feels like you’re being watched. Reality: You watched the first ad for 8 seconds. Signal = interest. So you get more hiking content. You engage again. Signal gets stronger. More ads follow. Not magic. Just feedback loops. The real concern: Meta doesn’t need to track your eyes. They already know: * What you’re interested in * When you’re likely to buy * What formats hook you * Who influences you This is more powerful than eye tracking. Because it’s based on actions, not attention guesses. The lesson for marketers: Stop worrying about infrared cameras. Focus on creative. Meta rewards ads that: * Hold attention * Drive engagement * Get clicks * Convert If your ad gets skipped in 0.5 seconds, it dies. If it gets watched and shared, it scales. The takeaway: Meta isn’t tracking your eyes. They’re tracking your behavior. And that’s what actually drives performance.
