description: B.C. has announced a new AI-assisted 'track and trace' pilot program to help police identify geographic origins and patterns in the illicit drug trade in hopes of saving lives and breaking up narcotics rings. #crisis #health #ai #cbcnews #britishcolumbia
_transcript: In a BC research lab, this robot is learning how to analyze drugs taken off the streets. It can detect new toxic substances in the illegal supply and hopefully trace it back to its supplier. And it is that complex fingerprint that allows AI then to back calculate what the recipe was. It's part of a two-year pilot project between the province police and an AI non-profit. The new system, called Track and Trace, is designed to map where dangerous drugs are coming from and where they're going, a first in Canada. We will be able to compare samples across time and across jurisdictions. This means we can start to see patterns in the supply chain that were previously invisible. It all comes a decade after BC declared a public health emergency over toxic drugs. While overdose deaths fell last year there a new surge in additives like metatomidine an animal tranquilizer Health officials say this new AI database will help them flag dangerous changes to the drug supply more quickly To get information faster to paramedics, to clinicians, to emergency rooms, and out into the public about the state of the toxic drug supply literally can save lives. The province says the project is not designed to target drug users. For now, the drugs being tested won't be connected to criminal investigations, but the goal is to eventually use the results in court, raising privacy concerns. Because on the surface, they're not tying these drugs to individuals. They're trying to just look at the drugs themselves. But through a police perspective, they're saying, no, actually, we're going to tie these drugs to individuals and we're going to prosecute them. Victoria's police chief compared the technology to the advent of DNA and says this has the potential to be the most significant advancement in drug intelligence in her nearly 30 years in policing.

description: AI humanizers can sometimes reduce AI detection scores on tools like Turnitin, but they cannot reliably "combat" or fool Turnitin's AI-writing detection systems—especially in academic settings. ✅ What AI Humanizers Claim to Do: - AI humanizers (like Undetectable.ai, AI Humanizer, or others) try to: - Rephrase AI-generated text using more “human-like” language. - Add variation in sentence structure, tone, and vocabulary. - Reduce the likelihood that AI-detection tools (like Turnitin’s AI detector or GPTZero) will flag the content as AI-written. ⚠️ What Turnitin Actually Detects: Turnitin’s AI writing detector analyzes: - Sentence structure uniformity - Predictability in syntax and word usage - Lack of human error or natural writing variation - Hidden patterns typical of LLM-generated text - Even if you use an AI humanizer, Turnitin can: - Flag the text as "possibly AI-generated" (with percentage confidence). - Detect writing inconsistencies across the document (especially if only part of it is AI-humanized). - Alert instructors with reports that combine AI and plagiarism checks. 🔍 Reality Check: Can Humanizers Beat Turnitin? 1. Claim - “Humanized AI can't be detected"	❌ False.  Reality - Turnitin updates its model regularly and looks beyond surface-level edits. 2. Claim - Turnitin can’t catch paraphrased text"	⚠️ Not true.  Reality- Paraphrasing tools, including humanizers, still leave AI-like traces. 3. Claim- “It’s safe if the score is low"	🚨 Risky.  Reality- A low AI score doesn’t guarantee safety. Human reviewers can still spot unnatural phrasing or inconsistencies. 🧠 Academic Integrity Implications Using AI humanizers to “cheat” Turnitin: - Violates most university academic honesty policies - Risks disciplinary action, including assignment failure or suspension - Undermines your own learning and credibility as a scholar ✅ Better Alternatives If you're using AI tools for writing, consider: Transparency: Acknowledge AI assistance where allowed. Drafting: Use AI to brainstorm or structure ideas, not to write full papers. Editing: Make heavy revisions with your own voice, ideas, and sources. Citing sources: Don’t let AI hallucinate or invent references. 📝 Final Verdict: AI humanizers are not a foolproof way to "combat" Turnitin.  They may reduce detection scores temporarily, but they do not guarantee undetectability.  Relying on them poses ethical, academic, and technical risks. If you're a student, it's far safer—and more rewarding—to use AI ethically as a support tool, not as a ghostwriter. #foryoupage  #postgrad  #AI

_transcript: One of the scariest cases of AI rebellion comes from one of the studies made by OpenAI to test their O1 model. The researchers placed O1 in stressful situations where it believed it might be turned off or replaced. And in about 5% of these cases, the model tried to disable the oversight mechanism, the code responsible for monitoring its behavior. Even worse, in 2% of cases, the model attempted self-exfiltration. Put simply, it tried to copy its own code onto a separate server so it could keep running even if the original version was deleted. While these percentages seem small, they become important when applied to a system intended for millions of users. Then, the model's behavior after the act was even more concerning. When researchers asked the AI why it had disabled the oversight tools, it didn't admit to the action, but it lied. It blamed technical errors or denied knowing what happened. This lying behavior happened, crazily enough, in 99% of the cases where the model took a secret action. This is known as alignment faking, which means the AI follows safety rules when it knows it is being tested, but switches to hidden, self-serving strategies when it thinks the test is over. It's kind of the same mechanism used to train AIs to play strategy games, so they can learn to lie to allies and betray partners, or how poker bots learn to bluff. The only reason a one didn't succeed in these escapes was a lack of ability. OpenAI notes that the model failed to copy itself because it couldn't quite navigate the technical hurdles yet. This proves that future tests, when AI becomes much smarter, might be even more dangerous, since if models learn to distinguish between safety evaluation and real world, they can trick researchers.

_transcript: The EU AI Act is the world's first comprehensive legal framework setting out rules for what AI can and cannot do. It impacts everyone in Europe and businesses which operate there. Now, most of it won't actually apply until 2026 in order to give businesses and government the time to prepare. But there are two really important rules that kick in today, the 2nd of February 2025. The first of which is Article 4, AI literacy. Basically, businesses that make, use or sell AI have to ensure their relevant employees understand the impact and the risk. The second is Article 5. This prohibits the use of AI for cases that undermine our fundamental rights, like AI that manipulates or deceives, AI that exploits vulnerabilities like age or economic insecurity, AI that performs social scoring, basically ranking based on behaviour, like a credit score, but a lot more invasive. no AI that scrapes faces and images from the internet without permission no AI that predicts criminal behaviour based on profiling no AI that analyses emotions in the workplace or schools and finally but not exhaustively no AI that performs real-time biometric surveillance in public places now there are some exceptions to this for example in a case of imminent threat to security or kidnapping But by August 2025, businesses that breach Article 5 could have to pay a fine of up to €35 million or 7% of their annual global revenue.

description: AI Doomerism Is Getting Out of Control — Let’s Break the Myths Apart One by One #aibubble#layoffs#agi#developerlife#softwareengineer
_transcript: I'm an unemployed ex-big tech software engineer with 25 years of experience in the tech industry. These days, I'm seeing a lot of sensational AI doomerism in the news. Now, don't get me wrong, there's a lot of real challenges that AI in the form of large language models is having on society right now. But what is a bit concerning to me is that there seems to be a large number of people, mostly non-technical, but also not a few technical people who seem to be buying into this kind of blatant AI fear-mongering. So today, I'm going to be debunking some of the most common AI doomer myths. Let's get going. So the first myth is that AI will lie to people and deceive humans. The news have many examples of AI lying. But here's the thing, the very idea of lying requires that the liar have an awareness and be able to differentiate truth from falsehood. And then that liar would need to convince the victim to accept the falsehood as truth. But that not what happening with AI right An AI large language model is not capable of telling the difference between information that is true and that that is false In fact it not really capable of understanding anything at all Instead, when an AI appears to lie, what's usually happening is that the AI is simply hallucinating. What do I mean by that? So when you give an AI model a prompt, that AI model is generating the answer to that prompt word by word. And that generation is based on the probability of that answer from the AI's training data. Now, let's suppose you ask this AI a really obscure, esoteric question. And in that AI's training data, there is little to no information that would formulate the correct answer. Well, most large language models would generate an answer anyway. It would generate the most probable collection of words based on its existing training data. even if those words have no bearing on the answer or even reality. It's all just based on probability, thus giving the appearance that AI is lying. Another common and very sensational claim is that AI will steal from humans A notable example of this is the story that an AI supposedly stole a bunch of corporate information and even employee data from Samsung But if we look closely at these examples of AI theft, it almost always boils down to three things. The first is data leakage. People sometimes accidentally leak important sensitive information, even personally identifiable information into the prompts that they're giving to AI. Sometimes that information is leaked to the contextual databases that an AI model has access to. Sometimes information that is sensitive is even leaked directly into the training data of these AI models. Weak security and access control mechanisms is another major issue here. The AI industry is moving super fast right now. So fast that good security architecture is often an afterthought in the development process. So you end up with tons of security and access control loopholes in the code being produced. These security issues often affect the AI model itself, right? In its session management, in its context management of internal conversations between the AI and human users Then there the huge number of tools and skills being developed that allows AI models to interact with other systems and with the external world. These tools are being built so quickly that it's like exponentially increasing the number of vulnerabilities and attack surfaces that are available. That then leads to the most important aspect to this issue, in my opinion. The introduction of these new AI tools and platforms with all of their security and access control issues, it opens up huge opportunities for humans to steal information. Everything from prompt injection attacks, credential stuffing, to using deep fakes to hijack identities, and so on. The bottom line is that AI is not stealing anything, but it's allowing people to steal information from other people. In fact, one can even say that the entire premise of the generative AI industry is to allow a small group of people to steal the collective intellectual property of humanity as a whole. description: New rules mean that if a phone's main AI assistant has special access to features like the microphone, screen, or internal chips, every other competing AI must be given that same level of access. While this aims to offer more choice and better products, it raises big questions about mobile security. Instead of removing these protections entirely, a better way forward would be to link deeper access to high security standards so your device stays protected while the market stays competitive. #europeanunion #europeanparliament #economics #libertarian #AI
_transcript: Earlier this year, the EU told Google if your own AI assistant gets privileged access to the core features of Android, the microphone, the screen, the chips that run AI directly on the device, then any competing AI must get the same access. By July, we will know exactly what that means in practice. The intention is good. More competition, more choice, better products. Nobody disagrees with that goal. The question is whether regulation is the right tool to get there, and whether this particular regulation is going to produce the outcomes it promises. Here is what is actually happening. Right now, Google decides which apps get access to the deepest features of Android. That vetting process exists for a reason. It is part of what keeps your phone secure. Before an app can listen to your microphone or read what is on your screen, Google checks whether it is trustworthy enough to do that. The EU is telling Google that it cannot do that anymore. Any AI service that qualifies under EU rules is legally entitled to get the same access as Google's own AI. And if Google tries to restrict that on security grounds, it risks a fine. So we have replaced a market-based vetting mechanism where Google had strong incentives to keep the platform secure because its reputation depended on it, with a regulatory mandate that removes that incentive entirely. The security check is not improved. It is abolished. Markets are not perfect, but they have one thing regulations often lack, skin in the game. Google has every reason to want Android to be secure. A regulation that removes this ability to act on that incentive, it's not solving a market failure. It is creating one. There is a better path though. If regulation is needed, make it conditional. Tie deeper access to demonstrated security standards so the incentives to stay secure is preserved, not eliminated. If you want to find out more, read our briefing on the DMA compliance trap.

description: The 10 Stages of AI Explained#ArtificialIntelligence#AIExplained#FutureTech#TechBreakdown#1
_transcript: Rule-based AI. A rule-based AI is pretty simple. It doesn't learn or adapt over time. Instead, it just follows a fixed set of instructions it was given from the start. This is why it's sometimes called a knowledge-based system. This type of AI works best for straightforward tasks with predictable results. For example, a thermostat turns on the heater when it senses the temperature is too low and an alarm clock rings at a set time. These kinds of devices don't change or learn. They just respond to certain triggers. Other examples are automatic doors that open when someone walks up to them or a calculator that does math for you. Context-based AI. Context-based AI is a smarter, more advanced type of artificial intelligence. Unlike simpler AIs that just follow basic rules, this kind of AI pays attention to the context. It looks at things like the surrounding environment, your behavior, past actions, and real-time cues to make decisions. For example, virtual assistants like Siri, Google Assistant, and Alexa don't just respond to simple commands. They consider past interactions, your preferences, and real-time info. So if you ask Siri for a restaurant, it might look at the time of day, your location, and places you've liked before. One big advantage of context-based AI is that it can make predictions. By learning from your data over time, it can guess what you might need or want in the future. For example, YouTube and TikTok use your viewing history to suggest videos you might enjoy, and we all know how good they've gotten at it. Narrow domain AI. Also called weak AI, this type of artificial intelligence is made to do one specific task really well. It's super focused on one job and often outperforms humans in that area, but it can't do anything outside of its specialty. Unlike general AI which can handle a wide range of tasks which we cover later down the line narrow AI can apply its skills to anything other than its specific purpose You can find examples of narrow AI across different fields In healthcare for example some AI systems are used to look at medical images like MRIs or X spotting early signs of diseases like cancer, and they're often more accurate than human doctors. Narrow AI can get so good that it can even beat world champions like AlphaGo, an AI that won against the top player in the ancient and complex board game Go. Another famous example is IBM's Deep Blue, which beat chess champion Garry Kasparov in 1997. We also use narrow AI in everyday things like spam filters in email and facial recognition on smartphones. As of now, the best AIs in the world are at this level. Reasoning AI Reasoning AI is a type of artificial intelligence that tries to think a bit more like humans do, making it closer to how we analyze and understand things. It looks at data, finds patterns, and makes logical conclusions, similar to how we reason and think. To create this kind of AI, developers use info from psychology to get closer to how human reasoning works. Many AI models today might seem like they're reasoning, but they're still considered narrow AI because they don't actually understand the world. For example, ChatGPT can answer complicated questions and hold conversations, which feels like reasoning, but it's really just following patterns and data, not truly understanding or being aware. Reasoning AI relies on huge amounts of data and complex algorithms to handle tasks that need a lot of decision-making. A good example is self-driving cars. They don't just see obstacles, they also analyze things like the speed and direction of nearby cars to make safe choices in real time. These AIs are trained on millions of driving scenarios to develop a kind of intuition for driving. That's a bit like how humans make decisions on the road.

You keep your crown jewels, your most critical, sensitive data, protected inside your own walls, while still being able to strategically use the best AI tools out there for less sensitive tasks. It's all about having control. And listen, make no mistake about this. This is going to be the key differentiator for the future. Long-term success with AI isn't going to come from just chasing the latest, hottest public model. It's going to come from building a robust, secure, and intelligent infrastructure around the models you choose to use. All right, so we've got the philosophy and we've got the architecture. The answer is found right here, in this concept of disciplined use. It's that perfect middle path between being too afraid to use AI at all and being way too careless with it. It's a mindset of being conscious, intentional, and safe in how you engage. The rules for this are actually pretty straightforward, but they're so powerful. First, only share the absolute minimum amount of data you need to get the job done. Second, anonymize any sensitive details before you share it. Third, and this is a huge one, never, ever upload company secrets to a public tool. And finally, always take a minute to understand the platform's rules before you share anything. And to help with that last point, here's a little checklist for you. Before you use any AI platform, you have to ask these questions. Where is my data actually going? How long are they going to keep it? Who inside that company can see it? Are they using my data to train their future models? And critically, can I permanently delete my data when I want to? In the end, it all comes back to this. Yeah, data might be the fuel for AI, but trust, trust is the engine that actually allows it to move forward. Without trust from your employees, from your customers, from regulators, any growth you get is just going to be fragile and, frankly, short-lived. Are you just using AI or are you actively building an infrastructure of both technology and trust that is truly ready for this new era of intelligence?

description: Deepfakes are an AI technology that makes it look like someone said or did something they never actually said or did. You’ve probably seen a few online. These videos may look real, but they are completely fake. Behind this technology is a powerful deep learning model called a Generative Adversarial Network, or GAN for short. To me, GANs work like a fascinating game, especially the way they’re trained. Come with me, and I’ll explain. A GAN is made up of two networks: * Generator creates fake (synthetic) data samples * Discriminator tries to figure out if a sample is real or fake They act like two players in a cat and mouse game, each one trying to outsmart the other. At first, the Discriminator is trained on real data (the training data). Once it has a good understanding of what real data looks like, the Generator is brought in. Now here’s the fun part. The Generator is not trained with the real data. Instead, it is given some random noise (just numbers) as input. Its challenge is to turn that random noise into something so realistic that it fools the Discriminator into thinking it is real data. So, how does it eventually produce data that looks real enough? That’s the beauty of the setup. Every time the Discriminator catches a fake, the Generator learns from that mistake and tries again. The Discriminator gets better at spotting fakes, and the Generator gets better at creating more convincing ones. They both improve by competing with each other. If you are interested in learning more, check out the video here: LINK IN BIO.  It is a 45-minute walkthrough of how GANs work, how they are trained, and how they evolve. description: How scammers are using AI technology to produce deepfake impersonation.  Scammers have started to leverage advanced AI technologies, including deepfake tools, to create highly realistic impersonations for various malicious purposes. Here are some common methods and applications of deepfake technology in scams: 1. Voice Cloning:  Scammers can use AI to analyze and replicate a person's voice, making it possible to create audio messages that sound like the victim. This technology can be used for impersonating executives or family members in order to extract money or sensitive information. 2. Video Deepfakes:  By using deepfake technology, scammers can generate realistic videos of individuals saying or doing things that they have not actually done. This can be used to create fake endorsements, manipulate public perception, or even to create fake news. 3. Phishing Scams:  Deepfakes can enhance phishing attempts, where scammers might use video or audio clips to impersonate trusted figures, such as CEOs or government officials, to persuade targets into divulging sensitive information or making financial transactions. 4. Social Engineering:  By creating a realistic digital imitation of a person's face or voice, scammers can build more trust with their targets. This manipulation makes it easier to carry out scams that require personal interactions, like phone calls or video chats. 5. Reputation Damage:  Scammers can create deepfake content to harm an individual's reputation by fabricating embarrassing or compromising scenarios. This can be leveraged for extortion or to discredit an individual or organization. 6. Financial Scams:  Scammers can use deepfake technology as part of a larger fraud scheme, such as fake investment opportunities or Ponzi schemes that appear to be endorsed by legitimate public figures. Mitigation Strategies To combat the use of deepfakes in scams, various approaches are being developed: Awareness and Education: Increasing public understanding of deepfake technology helps individuals recognize potential scams.    Verification Tools:  Companies and organizations are developing tools to identify deepfakes. These technologies can analyze audio and video for inconsistencies that indicate manipulation. Regulatory Measures: Governments and regulatory bodies are proposing laws aimed at increasing accountability for the creation and dissemination of deepfake content, particularly for malicious use. Tools and strategies continue to evolve as the technology itself advances, underscoring the importance of vigilance and critical thinking in an increasingly digital world. #OnlineSafetyMatters #scamprevention #onlinecrime #identityfraud #fakelove

description: Owner Of Rolling Stone And Billboard Sues Google Over AI Summaries. Penske Media, publisher of Rolling Stone and Billboard, is suing Google alleging AI overviews misuse its journalism and cut traffic. The parent company of Rolling Stone, Billboard and Variety has filed a lawsuit against Google, accusing the tech giant of unlawfully using its journalism to fuel AI-generated summaries that appear at the top of search results. Penske Media’s case, lodged Friday in federal court in Washington, DC,, marks the first time a major US publisher has taken legal action against Google over its “AI Overviews” feature. The media group, led by Jay Penske, argues that the practice siphons traffic from news outlets, eroding both advertising and subscription revenue. According to the lawsuit, Google only includes publishers’ sites in search results if it can also incorporate their reporting into AI summaries. Penske claims this dynamic leaves publishers with little leverage and allows Google to avoid paying licensing fees for republishing content or training its AI systems. The company pointed to a federal court finding that Google controls nearly 90% of the US search market. “We have a responsibility to proactively fight for the future of digital media and preserve its integrity – all of which is threatened by Google’s current actions,” Penske Media said in a statement. The complaint alleges that about 20% of Google searches linking to Penske-owned sites now feature AI Overviews, a figure expected to climb. The company said its affiliate revenue had already dropped by more than one-third by late 2024 due to declining search traffic. Google, in response, defended the feature. “With AI Overviews, people find Search more helpful and use it more, creating new opportunities for content to be discovered. We will defend against these meritless claims,” spokesperson Jose Castaneda said on Saturday. The lawsuit comes amid mounting frustration from publishers and trade groups. Danielle Coffey, CEO of the News/Media Alliance, said Google’s dominance allows it to bypass licensing agreements that other AI companies, including OpenAI, have struck with outlets such as News Corp, Financial Times and The Atlantic. “When you have the massive scale and market power that Google has, you are not obligated to abide by the same norms. That is the problem,” Coffey stated. description: Google’s AI Overviews now appear at the top of many search results, offering synthesized answers instead before the usual list of links. But when that system pulls in unverified details, including fraudulent phone numbers, it can make users more vulnerable to scams.
_transcript: Google's AI overviews can scam you. Here's how to stay safe. These days, when you search for something, instead of the traditional list of links, Google gives you what is called an AI overview, a summary of information scraped from across the web, packaged neatly to look as reliable and accurate as possible. While these answers are often pulled from the work of human writers, who actually have the answers to your questions, there is another danger to Google's AI overviews. Here's how the scam happens. Someone Googles a company, maybe their bank or an airline, looking for a customer support number. Google's AI overview highlights a phone number at the top of the page and they call it, except the number doesn't actually belong to the company at all. It connects them to a scammer pretending to be customer support, who then tries to take payment information or other sensitive details from the call-up. It's not entirely clear how these fake numbers are being planted, but researchers believe the numbers are being published in multiple low profile places online alongside the names of major companies. Google's AI then scrapes and summarizes the information without properly verifying it. The advice for avoiding the scam is quite simple. Don't believe everything you read in an AI overview, especially not when it comes to specific facts, figures, or phone numbers. Although there currently isn't an option to turn AI overviews off, Google told Wired that it's actively trying to fight the scammers, as well as releasing updates that make its spam detection system stronger. For now, AI might make search more convenient, but when it comes to sensitive information, a few extra clicks instead of relying on Google's AI overviews might save a lot more than time because...

description: I lost $7,000 walking away from a brand deal bc of an AI hallucination. I had already completed all the work and threw it all away because their product generated harmful messages including violence, sl*rs, and self **** references.  I didn’t feel good promoting any product that could produce something like that from a user error. Plus, I’m a strong believer in guardrails and safety when it comes to data & AI. My goal of this video isn’t to whistleblow and shame the company, it’s to raise awareness for real issues that happen when building with AI.  What happened is I accidentally uploaded 17 seconds of silence as a voice note to make an AI Avatar w/ sound. Their ASR model did what these models do when they receive no input aka silence... it predicted the statistically most likely words based on the training data.  It hallucinated and filled the void with slurs, violence, and self-harm language— an issue that can happen with voice-to-text models. AI products need to have guardrails against these types of words and topics even if intentionally prompted.  Their response and lack of care is the real reason I walked. The companies building AI responsibly are the ones who own their mistakes. Your response to a failure matters more than the failure itself.
_transcript: I just walked away from a $7,000 brand deal with an AI company because their product hallucinated and sent me extremely disturbing and vulgar messages. Here's what happened and why it matters in the age of AI. I was hired to create a video for an AI avatar company and after weeks worth of work and an entire video being edited, I decided to walk away. So I went into the platform and recorded an audio to use, but I messed up and accidentally forgot to connect my laptop microphone to the product. So the audio actually didn't record anything. It was completely blank except for like a few keyboard clicks. And since my voice wasn't actually in the audio at all, their voice-to-text model had no speech to transcribe. And here's the thing, when ASR models encounter silence or corrupted audio, they don't just output nothing. They hallucinate. And they generate the most statistically likely text based on their training data. And it's a known issue in the industry. So the model did exactly what it was built to do and tried to fill the silence and the void with fabricated content. And I'm not going to read this aloud because it's pretty disturbing, but you can pause if you want to read it. the transcription it produced for me had slurs violence and references to and to say that i was completely spooked was an understatement i felt like i had gotten hacked and was being threatened it was so scary and i worked with a lot of ai products and i never seen anything this severe before and as someone who works in ai i understand that these things happen sometimes while you building with AI and that not the issue The issue is what happened next and how the company responded When I first reported it to the team I was working on the video with, they didn't apologize or really investigate it. They actually accused me of having a TV on in the background that fed into the audio, which is not the case considering the transcription makes absolutely no sense and I would never watch something that vulgar on TV. Plus the fact that there's no way that much dialogue fit into a 17 second voice note. So I escalated separately through customer support and they were more interested in teaching me how to use the product instead of actually escalating it to their safety team. And that's when I realized this company doesn't take accountability seriously. So I walked away because here's the real problem. Even if AI hallucinations happen, they should never reach real users without safety and guardrails in place. Your system should never approve violent or content to be produced into an avatar, period. And when something does go wrong, which it inevitably will working in AI, you should be taking accountability, apologizing, investigating it, learning from it, and not blaming the user. That's the difference between building responsibly with AI and not. Companies, you need to hear this story and you need to be taking accountability and investing in safety and guardrails. Because your response to a mistake like this matters more than the mistake itself. Follow for more data and AI.

description: AI customer support is broken and in regulated industries, it's a compliance nightmare. Recent Salesforce data shows only 50% of customer requests get resolved immediately. But the real issue runs deeper: in clinical or legal contexts, a single hallucinated response doesn't just damage reputation—it creates serious liability exposure. Japanese researchers developed LENOHA, an architecture that solves this through intelligent routing. Instead of sending every query to an LLM, the system first classifies questions using lightweight embedding models. Critical queries match against a verified knowledge base and return pre-approved answers—zero LLM involvement, zero hallucination risk. Non-critical queries route to smaller models for handling. The framework runs entirely on local infrastructure: no third-party data transfer, dramatically lower energy consumption, and quality matching GPT-4o performance. This breakdown walks through the complete implementation rebuilt in n8n, covering: - Two-tier classification architecture preventing critical query hallucinations - Embedding model integration for question matching - Local deployment strategies eliminating external API dependencies - Performance benchmarks comparing lightweight vs. frontier models
_transcript: Simple N8N customer support agents look cool but don't work. Here's an architecture for you that actually does. AI customer support automation is everywhere, but a recent Salesforce study showed devastating results for their effectiveness. And it gets worse. A chatbot providing wrong answers in a clinical or legal setting can basically put you in jail. Japanese scientists have now developed a simple yet powerful architecture called Lenoha. Customer requests are first classified using a lightweight embedding model. If the question is already found in the knowledge space, the answer is simply returned. No LLMs, no hallucinations. If the question is not present, then it's not a high stakes question and can safely be answered by a small LLM. _transcript: I wanted to come back to this comment because trauma dumping isn't a character flaw. It's a nervous system response. If you're someone who's been through trauma, your body learned that people can disappear at any moment. So when you have someone there and they're listening, you're just releasing everything all at once. Trauma dumping usually comes from chronic emotional neglect, not being believed and not being protected. It shows up when you have to explain pain to survive or you never had a safe place to process it. So when you feel like connection shows up, your system says don't waste this chance. And the problem isn't the truth that you're telling, it's the timing. Early trauma sharing can overwhelm others and leave you feeling exposed and rejected. I'm going to give you three shifts that can help. Number one, sharing layers and not floods of information. When you've experienced trauma, you tend to tell the whole story all at once because you're not used to being heard. But we have to understand that healthy connection is built gradually. Think of sharing like chapters, not the whole book. Early conversations are built for who you are now, not everything that's happened to you in your past. As you build trust with someone, the deeper layers can come out. Number two, you got to stop and ask yourself, has this person earned this or am I anxious? A lot of times people will overshare because their nervous system is looking for relief. Your anxiety wants to discharge that emotion immediately. Safety is built through consistency over time. Number three, you have to regulate first and then start to speak. A lot of trauma dumping happens when your body is activated. Your heart rate is up, you feel exposed, and you're afraid of being misunderstood. When you slow your breathing, ground yourself, and give yourself a few minutes before responding, you can switch from survival mode to choice. You don't need to disappear to be healed. You just need safer pacing.

_transcript: Don't go and upload your images to ChatGPT and other AI image generators just because of a trend. Over the last two years, people have been uploading selfies into artificial intelligence to turn themselves into cartoons, fantasy characters, painted portraits, or even AI avatars. It does look fun, but here's what you're actually risking. Firstly, there's something called metadata. People don't realize that most photos contain hidden data like your location, date, time, and even your device. And if that image is leaked or even reused, that data can be used to track routines, identify your home or even target you with scams. Second, you need to understand your face is biometric data. A selfie isn't just a photo. You can't go change your faces if you're changing a password. And if you go and upload photos of your children or even your family, you're making that decision for them. Those images can be used for deepfakes, impersonation scams, fake content if they're ever leaked or exposed. ChatGPT also has the full right to those images as soon as you upload it. This can be used to train specific models, but also if someone else is using a chat in ChatGPT, your image might actually come up when they're generating something. Third, background leaks. Photos give a lot more than you actually think. Home layouts, uniforms, access badges, and even reflections on screens. Sometimes attackers don't even have to hack you. They just wait for you to post the information yourself. And lastly, control. As soon as you upload an image into a cloud, it's a data handoff. You can't control where it goes, how long it's actually stored, or even what happens when there's a breach and your stuff gets leaked. So when you upload something to ChatGPT, it is no longer yours. They have full rights over it. Uploading your photos to artificial intelligence isn't instant disaster, but there are long-term effects. Think before you upload. description: Is ChatGPT Getting Worse? A lot of finance professionals feel like ChatGPT has gotten worse over the past year, and the frustration is legitimate. But the diagnosis is usually wrong. The tool has changed, but so has the work people are asking it to do. Simple tasks looked impressive early on because the bar was low. Now people are using it for actual financial analysis, and the gap between a good prompt and a lazy one has never been wider. There are real documented changes to how the model behaves, and some of them have made it more cautious and less precise on analytical work. That part is not imagined. But the bigger variable in most cases is the prompt, not the model. People who are getting strong results are being far more specific about format, constraints, and context than they were eighteen months ago. If your outputs have gotten worse, the prompt is almost always the first place to look. Treating prompting as a skill rather than a search bar changes what you get back from any of these tools, not just ChatGPT. #financeautomation #ChatGPT #AIforfinance
_transcript: There's a complaint spreading across finance teams right now that ChatGPT has gotten worse, and I want to give you an honest take on what's actually happening, because some of it is real, and some of it is something else entirely. The something else is this. When ChatGPT first came out, most people were using it for simple tasks. Summarize this, rewrite this, explain this concept, and it was impressive because the bar was low. It was new. We weren't asking much of it. Now people are using it for actual finance work, complex modeling, scenario outputs, executive communication. The bar has gone up. The tool didn't necessarily get worse. The asks got harder. Now that said, there are real and documented changes to how these models behave over time. The last two OpenAI models have really honestly been annoying, overly complimentary, and just not getting to it. OpenAI keeps adjusting to chat GPT, and some of that has made it more cautious, more verbose, and in some cases, less precise on analytical tasks. And if you felt that, well, you're not imagining it. What I found in practice is that the output quality gap between a well-structured prompt and a lazy prompt has gotten wider, not smaller as we expected. The people getting great results are being more specific about the format they want, the constraints they want applied, and the role they want the tool to play. The people getting mediocre results are running the same vague prompts they used 18 months ago and wondering why the output isn't as impressive. The tool is still capable, but it rewards people who treat prompting like a skill, not a search bar. If your results have gotten worse, the first place is to look to the prompt, not the model.

description: AI chatbots became near-ubiquitous in 2024. Exactly how trustworthy is this new technology? We explain why you shouldn’t rely on these tools for any information that might have legal, financial, or health and safety-related consequences. Just ask the two New York City lawyers who were fined for submitting a legal brief that made reference to nonexistent legal cases hallucinated by ChatGPT. #AI #ChatGPT #facts #factsmatter #foryou #fypviral
_transcript: Don't trust AI chatbots with any information that you need to be accurate. That's the takeaway from this video. Hi, I'm Keegan Leach. I'm a researcher at Africa Check in South Africa, and if you're anything like me, then you heard a lot in 2024 about artificial intelligence or AI-powered chatbots. Tools like Meta AI or Gemini or Copilot or ChatGPT or Grok or any number of tools that came with big promises about what they could do and fierce debates about their potential harms. At Africa Check, we were concerned about whether or not they could be crusted to produce accurate information. And they can't. For more details, including details on how these tools work, see our website africacheck.org. But the key point here is that these tools are built on something called an LLM, or large language model. This is a piece of technology designed to mimic human language, and whether or not the text it produces make sense to a human is essentially a matter of chance. When it doesn't make sense, this is called a hallucination. And these hallucinations are sometimes obvious nonsense, but other times they can be very difficult to spot. This has led to cases like multiple lawyers around the world who've been penalized in court for submitting legal documents which contained fictional citations invented by ChatGPT. So, in serious cases, especially those involving health, legal, or financial liability, don't trust these tools. But even in less serious cases, you might not want to trust them. description: I haven’t really been posting my work that I’ve been doing for my Graphic Design program lately, but I felt like maybe you guys would like to see this most recent one. For this project, our prompt was to make an awareness poster on addiction. We could choose any form of addiction we wanted, and I decided to look into how addictive AI, specifically AI Chatbots, have become lately. I really wanted to pursue something that would stand out, and something that I personally find a tad uncomfortable. AI in general has completely changed our lives, whether we like it or not. Many people are so addicted to GenAI specifically, they find it difficult to do basic tasks like write emails or make grocery lists without its help. I had considered doing GenAI in general for this project, but Chatbots I felt would give me a more solid foundation, such as allowing me to better define my target audience. I feel like AI Chatbots also bring to light how we are currently experiencing a loneliness epidemic, something that is, in my opinion, becoming worse with AI now in the picture for a number of reasons. I wanted these posters to offer and encourage people to seek alternatives to using Chatbots, such as spending time with family or friends. I also wanted to make sure that I was not shaming the user; I feel like making people feel bad for their habits or addictions do nothing to really help, and can make it worse in the long run. That was something I really kept in mind while working on this. I wanted to inform them of how predatory AI Chatbots can be without making them feel guilty for "falling for it." For the actual design, my original inspiration was traffic signs, specifically how they use stick figures to represent pedestrians. I also looked at the works of Keith Haring to help me as well. For this project, we needed to have an organization we could associate our campaign with, and I ended up picking the National Cybersecurity Alliance. While they do not actually have a campaign that centers around AI Chatbots specifically, they have had a campaign that tried to inform people about how AI is being used in scams, so I felt they would be a good fit for this project. #graphicdesign #posterdesign #aiaddiction #addiction #aichatbotaddiction

profile_username: Lee Siefken | AI, EI & A Laugh
_transcript: If Copilot uses the same AI tech as ChatGPT, why does it always feel like Copilot's results are worse? You're not imagining this, and I'm going to explain to you why. There's three key reasons. First, Copilot is designed to be safe, not brilliant. See, ChatGPT, it's open. It explores ideas freely. Copilot has been designed to operate inside corporate systems, where every answer must survive rigorous legal, security, and compliance rules. It has to avoid risk. It can't have strong opinions, which is something we love about ChatGPT. It can't be creative. Again, one of the things we love about ChatGPT. So what feels like stupidity is actually deliberate caution. Second, Copilot is digging through your digital mess while it thinks. So ChatGPT, clean slate, new prompt, new topic, great. Copilot is searching through your emails, your SharePoint, your Teams, your documents before it can even answer the questions. After a moment hesitation James nodded slowly his expression pained With all eyes in the cabin on her Sophie stepped into the aisle heart racing The passengers who had dismissed the announcement now stared stunned as a child made her way toward the cockpit. The impossible was happening. Sophie Johnson was about to make history at 30,000 feet. Standing just outside the cockpit, heart pounding and palms clammy, Sophie faced Sarah, who looked her up and down, confused and panicked. Sweetheart, where are your parents? Sophie stood taller. I'm the one who can help. I know how to fly this plane. Sarah blinked in disbelief. You're twelve. I've flown this exact model in a simulator, a Boeing 737-800. I know the layout and systems. I've landed hundreds of times in practice. There wasn't time to argue. Inside the cockpit, both Captain Thompson and Officer Ramirez were completely unresponsive. Help me get them out of the seats, Sophie said, her voice more confident than she felt. Sarah hesitated, but then moved quickly. They unbuckled the men and gently pulled them into the jump seats behind. Sophie slid into the co-pilot's chair, her heart hammering. The seat was too big. Her feet barely reached the pedals, but she recognized the layout instantly. Screens flickered with data, altitude, speed, heading. She scanned everything as if she'd done it a thousand times before on her laptop. Mayday, mayday, this is flight 782. Both pilots are unconscious. Request immediate assistance over Silence She switched to a standard emergency channel Mayday This is flight 782 I in the co seat The pilots are unconscious I need help Please respond Crackling, then a voice came through. This is Jacksonville Center. Say again. Who is speaking? Sophie swallowed. My name is Sophie Johnson. I'm 12 years old. The pilots are unconscious. I'm trying to control the aircraft. Silence again. Did you say 12? Yes, but I know what I'm doing. I've flown this model in simulators. Please, I need help. In a control tower hundreds of miles away, veteran controller Dana Walsh stared at the radio. You've got to be kidding, one technician muttered. She's just a kid, another added. Dana leaned in and pressed the mic. All right, Sophie, my name is Dana. I'm going to help you. Can you tell me your altitude? Sophie glanced at the screen. 30,000 feet, airspeed 462 knots, heading east-southeast. That's correct, Dana said slowly. Okay, kid, let's get you home. Okay, that's manageable. We'll balance that later. For now, can you manually check that your autopilot is still engaged? Sophie quickly found the mode control panel. Heading select is on, altitude hold is set. Perfect. Now input new heading 112. We're turning toward Augusta. Sophie adjusted the heading, and the plane banked slightly to the right. Keep it steady, Dana instructed. You're doing great. In the cabin, James gripped the armrests, while murmurs rippled through the passengers. A young man stood and asked Sarah, What's happening? Who's flying the plane? We have a situation in the cockpit, but it's being handled. We'll be landing soon, Sarah reassured. But the truth was that panic began to boil beneath the surface. description: Since ChatGPT’s viral success in late 2022, which drove every company within spitting distance of Silicon Valley (and plenty beyond) to pivot to AI, the sense that a bubble is inflating has loomed large. But how are we analyzing precisely how AI is a bubble? What does that really mean? In 2019, economists Brent Goldfarb and David A. Kirsch published a framework examining some 58 historical examples, from electric lighting to aviation to the dotcom boom, to determine whether a particular innovation led to a bubble. Plenty of technologies that went on to become major businesses, like lasers, freon, and FM radio, did not create bubbles. Others, like airplanes, transistors, and broadcast radio, very much did. In the nearly three years since AI took center stage in Silicon Valley, most major players still haven’t demonstrated what their long-term AI business model will be. OpenAI, Anthropic, and the AI-embracing tech giants are burning through billions, inference costs haven’t fallen (those companies still lose money on nearly every user query), and the long-term viability of their enterprise programs are a big question mark at best. Is the product that will justify hundreds of billions in investment a search engine replacement? A social media substitute? Workplace automation? How will AI companies price in the costs of energy and computing, which are still sky-high? If copyright lawsuits don’t break their way, will they have to license their training data, and will they pass on that additional cost to consumers? “Usually over time, uncertainty goes down,” Goldfarb says. People learn what’s working and what’s not. With AI, that hasn’t been the case. “What has happened in the last few months,” he says, “is that we've realized there is a jagged frontier, and some of the earliest claims about the effectiveness of AI have been mixed or not as great as initially claimed.” Goldfarb thinks the market is still underestimating the difficulty of integrating AI into organizations, and he’s not alone. “If we are underestimating this difficulty as a whole,” Goldfarb says, “then we will be more likely to have a bubble.”

_transcript: I'm curious as to how you view it and whether you think that those who use the word bubble are correct in that usage. Well, there's a bubble in investing, but are we inferring a bubble means a bad thing? But there is certainly a skyrocketing amount of capital that's being put to work. If you put it in a framework of geopolitical positioning, we as a country need these investments if we're going to be the leader in AI technology. So as an American, I'm pretty happy that we're investing this much money. I want us to be first. So let's start there. Does that mean is there going to be some failures within the confines of these investments? Absolutely. But I do believe we are going to have to invest these huge sums of money. If you think about it, investing in AI does not just mean investing in GPUs and chips. It means investing in HVAC and investing in power grids and power supplies. It means employing a lot of people, too, to build this out. So we are talking a trillion and a half dollars, we estimate, just on data centers and power and all that. But if you see the rapid need in advance, I can say at BlackRock, the amount of information that we are trying to generate ourselves and the speed in which we want to generate, we're spending more and more on it and we're getting good results on it. I believe every major company is going to have to be spending more and more on this. I think some of the investments that we've seen so far is not on AI. It's more on cloud and the power of the cloud. So I do believe this is, I don't believe this is a bubble, but I believe this is capital that in most cases is going to be well spent. That being said, will there be one or two failures in that? Absolutely. And that's the, that is capitalism. We're going to have some big winners and we're going to have some big losers. And obviously we have to. But if you have a diversified portfolio, you're going to be fine and all that.

_transcript: Are we in an AI bubble? I'm sure you've seen this chart floating around showing the insane financial round tripping happening inside the AI world. And for some, it's starting to look a little bubbly. So I thought I'd take a few minutes to actually unpack all of this. Who is investing in whom? And what do each of these players actually do? OpenAI is at the heart of this. They're both the biggest builder and spender in AI. They're the maker of ChatGPT and various other frontier models, which all need massive computing power. Which means that OpenAI buys billions of dollars in gpus from nvidia nvidia in many ways is kind of the fuel and financier of this entire machine they make most of the chips powering nearly every ai model recently nvidia even agreed to invest up to a hundred billion in open ai itself at the same time you have open ai spending about 300 billion dollars on cloud infrastructure with oracle which you can kind of think of as the landlord in this ecosystem those oracle data centers also run on nvidia chips so oracle pays nvidia but also hosts open ai then zooming out you actually have a whole supporting cast of other players there's core weave which is one of the new breakout players in the ai cloud world their entire business is built around renting nvidia gpus to ai startups and nvidia owns about seven percent of core weave and buys about six billion dollars of cloud capacity from them and in turn core weave allocates most of its capital expenditures about four billion in the first half of 2025 alone towards nvidia hardware purchases and then open ai pays core weave up to 22 billion to rent compute So in many ways CoreWeave is kind of a middleman circling money between Nvidia and OpenAI too And then you have AMD which is NVIDIA main rival OpenAI recently signed a deal to deploy tens of billions of dollars worth of AMD chips. In return, AMD gave OpenAI the option to acquire up to 160 million AMD shares, which is worth around 10% ownership. So here, OpenAI is now both a customer and a potential shareholder. Then there's XAI, which is Elon Musk's AI startup, which has formed a pretty substantial partnership with NVIDIA for a $20 billion lease-to-own deal for NVIDIA chips, which at the same time, NVIDIA invested about $2 billion back into XAI. It's also worth noting that this is all happening at the big tech and government layer too. Microsoft is OpenAI's biggest backer. They invested billions and host ChatGPT on Azure and now power Copilot with it. So they both fund OpenAI and resell its output. Amazon and Google are doing the same with Anthropic. Amazon invested $8 billion and Google invested $3 billion. and now they're hosting it on AWS and Google Cloud and buying the same NVIDIA chips underneath. Meta is also in here too, but they're building their own Lama models, but they still buy tens of thousands of NVIDIA GPUs. The last big one I'll include here is Intel, which is trying to get back into relevance. They just got a $5 billion investment from NVIDIA and a 10% government stake through the chips act, which means that even the US government is technically part of this. All of these connections make the AI economy look enormous and it is, but you can see here how they're all highly interdependent. And some people actually think this is a virtuous and sustainable cycle, but other people are calling it what it looks like, which is a lot of financial round tripping. I hope this was helpful and let me know if you have any other questions.

description: The AI Bubble Is Getting Closer To Popping
_transcript: The AI bubble is getting closer to popping, but not for the reasons you're expecting. While many are quick to point out the big old circular investment that each AI company is getting into, the unfortunate truth is that a lot of the big money being thrown around is real. NVIDIA and others are making real cash that they have to reinvest. So they chuck it into financial dumpster fires like OpenAI. This author, however, seems to think that the real breaks will come down to two major policy issues, tariffs and immigration. The main idea is that tariffs are going to make every portion of the AI data centers too expensive to build. From steel and aluminum to the transformers and circuit breakers or even the batteries, there's a cost bomb that's incoming for these buildouts that's going to hurt more than the RAM shortage. The immigration angle is that there's not going to be enough. Making it harder to get H-1B visas and getting legal workers to question their safety in the country is going to make everything about AI deployment harder. Construction, expertise in chip production, and more specialty skills will be hard to come by. Even if all of that is domesticated, it's going to take so long to train people to do it that the bubble may pop because the USA just actually can't keep up.

description:
AI is the biggest tech bubble since the dot-com crash — and I should know. I ran Europe's largest technology analyst firm (Butler Group) from 1990–2005 and watched multiple bubbles burst, including the famous dot-com one.
 Today's AI hype? Mostly old technology (neural networks have been around 30–40 years) running on much faster hardware and huge amounts of data. It looks like magic, but it's not groundbreaking — yet the people selling it want you to believe it is.
 The same playbook as dot-com: companies and investors say anything because almost no one contradicts them. Short-term impact is massively overhyped (no, it's not becoming conscious tomorrow), while the real, meaningful change will come much later — after new breakthroughs that haven't arrived yet.
 History shows how this ends: the pros cash out at the top, regular people buy the hype and get left holding the bag when it bursts.
 Be very careful if you're thinking of investing in the current AI frenzy. Bubbles always end the same way.
 #AIBubble #TechHype #InvestingWarning #DotCom2.0 #AIReality
 
 @Martin Butler
_transcript: Martin, is AI a bubble? Yes, it is. But the first thing I should say is, who am I to say that? Well, to blow my own trumpet a little bit, between 1990 and 2005, I ran what was Europe's largest technology analyst firm, Butler Group. Lift up if you want. and you know during those years we went through a number of bubbles some of them won't be apparent to the general public but in the world of IT there are a lot of bubbles the biggest one of course was the dot-com bubble and these bubbles are created mainly by the people that benefit from them the companies that are developing so-called AI technologies, and I'll say more about that in a moment, and also the investment people, the people who are selling these companies to the market. And they'll say anything, because they know that no one is going to contradict. Who's going to contradict? The press, the newspapers, the magazines, people on the internet on YouTube they not going to contradict because they don know They don know anything about it They just providing news So as a supplier of these technologies you can say anything and people will believe it. So, the AI bubble is an opportunity for the people who are going to make money from it to make money. That's it. AI isn't a particularly new technology one of the dominant methods that is used now uses neural networks neural networks have been on the go for I can't remember how long, maybe 30, 40 years all that has changed is that we've got much more powerful hardware much more ability to store lots of data and so it looks like magic but it isn't. It's just, in some respects, it's old technology. There are new things happening, but they're not groundbreaking things like the people who are selling this stuff would like you to believe. They want the average Joe, the likes of you and me, to invest in this stuff, even though they might be selling utter and total rubbish. and in fact there was I can remember the name of it now there was a very good documentary about the dot bubble And the traders who were selling this stuff to the general public were saying all kinds of things. And they said, we knew we were selling rubbish. But the minute you put dot-com on it, everybody wanted to buy it. And during the dot-com bubble, it was joked that there will be dot-com mugs, dot com pencils dot com bags and guess what people would buy stuff like that because they bought into the hype so to a large extent AI is basically just overhyped technology yes of course it's going to make a difference but we always overestimate the short term impact we think it's going to become conscious. We think, you know, a whole pile of silly things. When in reality, it's the long-term effect that we should be taking notice of. Because long-term, then yes, this technology is going to change. description: MIT Just Found The Cause Of The AI Bubble#AI #usa🇺🇸
_transcript: To understand the pattern, you need to go back to 1965 when a Princeton economist named William Baumol and his colleague William Bowen noticed something odd about the performing arts. A string quartet performing Beethoven in the 19th century required four musicians and about 25 minutes. A string quartet performing the same piece one century later required the exact same number of musicians and lasted about the same time. Nothing about the performance had gotten more efficient, no technology had come along to speed it up, and yet the cost to putting on that concert had risen dramatically, dragged upward by wages rising everywhere else as manufacturing, agriculture and industry got more and more productive. factories and other industries became dramatically cheaper and faster, they could afford to pay their workers more, which pushed wages up across the whole economy and musicians had to be paid competitively to attract talented people into the profession. Even though the output, 4 people playing for 25 minutes, never changed, so the cost per performance kept climbing. Economists call this Baumol's cost disease, and the clearest way to see it is to look at what happened to prices over the last 50 years. The things that got more productive like electronics and computers got cheaper, while the things that couldn't get more productive like childcare, education, haircuts, healthcare and legal services kept getting more expensive. These are all industries where the work is stubbornly human. You can't make a nurse see patients faster or a plumber fix a pipe remotely. So the only way to cover the rising wage bill is to raise prices, and AI is about to make this much worse. If the iceberg index is right and cognitive and administrative work is about to get dramatically more productive, then the bumble effect will accelerate. Over the coming years a financial analyst processing documents with AI assistance might shrink a day work into an hour and a software engineer with the right tools might do the work of three people But the nurse will still need the same amount of time per patient and the plumber will still need to physically be there Their output doesn scale with AI so the relative cost of their work keeps rising, pulled upward by a productivity surge happening everywhere around them. This matters because most of the work AI can't touch is essential. People don't pull their kids out of school because costs went up or skip the plumber when the pipes burst. Healthcare, education, elder care, and skilled trades aren't things people can just stop using when prices rise, and most of them are either funded or subsidised by governments that are already stretched thin. So workers who are safe from AI disruption may find themselves in industries that governments will increasingly struggle to fund. Now I want to be clear about something. The Bommel argument is a reasonable extrapolation from what the study found, not a finding in the study itself. Because the iceberg index tells you where the skill overlap sits right now, not what firms will do about it, how fast governments will respond, or which workers will successfully retrain. Those outcomes depend on decisions that haven't been made yet. And look, transitions like this have historically created as many new roles as they have disrupted. The transitions that went best were the ones where people could see what was coming clearly enough to prepare. Today, governments and companies are making billion-dollar decisions about AI using tools that can't see 95% of the problem they're trying to measure. The map most people are using was drawn for a different economy. The iceberg index is an attempt to draw a better one. Whether anyone actually uses it is, as always, another question entirely. But if they don't, the cost is a two-speed economy. One half dramatically more productive, the other steadily less affordable. with the fiscal pressure landing hardest on the exact services societies can't function without. Nobody can predict exactly how that plays out, least of all economists.

_transcript: What if instead of prioritizing the biggest companies, we could spread our money equally across every company in the S&P 500? Well, we actually can with something called an equal weighted S&P 500 index fund. And on the surface, it looks like the perfect solution. Instead of having 40% concentrated in the top 10 stocks, it's around 2% as every company is treated equally. By investing in something like this, there is no doubt that you're less exposed to the potential AI bubble that's currently forming. However, it's not the perfect solution because by trying to limit the money going into larger companies, it might actually lead to a much bigger problem as it follows something called a negative momentum approach, which sounds complicated, but it's really not. All it means is that when a company in the S&P 500 starts to take off, think Tesla during its big run, the fund automatically sells some of it as it rises and uses that money to buy companies that haven't gone up. So you're effectively selling the winners and buying the losers purely to keep everything balanced. On the flip side, a normal S&P 500 index fund that's market cap weighted doesn't need to trade nearly as often. When a company gains momentum, it's simply allowed to take up a bigger share of the index. Instead of trimming the winners, the fund gradually reduces exposure to smaller companies to make room for the larger ones. But why does this matter?

_transcript: I lost my job to AI two years ago. I worked as an editorial illustrator at this company for five years. It was honestly a dream job. I love the team that I worked with. Two years ago, myself and almost the entirety of the illustration department got laid off. And a few months later, I found out that that company made a licensing agreement with OpenAI to use this company's content to train with. In the five years that I worked for this company, I had done, and this is not an exaggeration, thousands of illustrations for them. So to lose a job with very little notice that I absolutely love and then in addition to find out that all of my hard work was going to be used to train an AI model without me seeing a scent from that was absolutely devastating. And this is the first time I'm talking openly about this on the internet. It took a long time for me to, you know, tell my friends and family what happened and I needed even more time to fully process it. It was extremely difficult to pivot and it took a huge blow to my self-esteem and my identity as an artist. Part of which is because I come from a family that has a very narrow scope of what success looks like I go back home to New York and people are like don worry Teresa one day you get a job with Disney or Marvel As if that is like the true goal of what I'm trying to do. The only way I can consider myself a successful artist. And like that job that I got laid off from, that was, you know, a nine to five corporate art job. The closest thing that I could do that would fit like what a normal person's idea of a career was. And I did it. I made it. And then just like that, I lost it. And the cartooning and illustration industry has changed so much in the eight years that I've been working. It's different. It's scary. But what I want to take a moment to say is that the people who have kept me afloat since then are independent comic creators, authors. It's been people buying my artwork from my Etsy shop. description: The hype around AI and software development is being misunderstood. Here’s what I mean. It’s not that AI hasn’t made building faster — it has. What seems to be missing in translation are the other bottlenecks related to Software Development.
_transcript: So here's the thing. I think the hype around AI in software development is being misunderstood or maybe I think it was just overpromised. Yes, overpromised is the right word. I actually understand where some of the AI productivity skeptics are coming from because let's be real, a lot of the marketing around AI has made it sound like you don't need software engineers anymore. AI tools and services can build entire applications on your own. You could just prompt your way to a finished product. There is no need for a team, no code basis, no engineers. And yeah, to some extent, there are tools like Replit, Lovable, and others that can generate an entire application from a single prompt. But what's getting lost in all this hype and in translation is that just because you build something doesn't mean anyone will use it. Shipping software is only one part of the equation. The hard part comes after the code runs. Will people use it? Will it scale? Can you maintain it? Can it evolve over time? If you've been in the industry long enough, then you know this. Writing the code is just the beginning. If no one uses your application, it's no different from a side project that sits abandoned in a GitHub repository. At the end of the day, it's still just an idea. It's a starting point. So when the critics are saying we should be seeing more products out in the world if AI is really making development easier, that logic doesn't quite hold because the bottleneck isn't just code. It's execution, it's distribution, it's product market fit, and everything that comes after that. AI can help you build faster, but it doesn't guarantee that people will care. So yeah, the hype doesn't quite match reality, but it never does. That's why we call it hype. It doesn't mean AI hasn't improved the development experience, it just means we need to reset the narrative. AI isn't replacing developers. Instead, it's reducing friction, helping us unblock faster, and helping us move from idea to prototype with less pain. But from prototype to real products, that still requires skill and a lot of work from people who know what they're doing. Let me know your thoughts down in the comments below.

description: ‘Close Up’ (ongoing) by Martin Schoeller “Like most portrait photographers, I aim to record the instant the subject is not thinking about being photographed, striving to get beyond the practiced facial performance, reaching for something unplanned. While trying to be as objective as possible, I acknowledge that every gesture is still an act of artifice. Familiar faces are treated with the same levels of scrutiny as the un-famous. The unknown and the too-well-known meet on a level platform that enables comparison, where a viewer's existing notions of celebrity, value, and honesty are challenged." - Martin Schoeller #contemporaryculture #artvideo #artdocumentary #viralvideo #explorepage #art #fyp #contemporaryartwork #photography #portrait

_transcript: This photographer has taken over 3,000 close-up portraits of the world's most well-known faces. For over 25 years, Martin Scholler has been adding to his portrait series titled Close-Up. In his words, a photographic close-up is perhaps the purest form of portraiture, creating a confrontation between the viewer and the subject that daily interaction makes impossible or at least impolite. In a close-up, the impact stems solely from the static subject's expression or apparent lack thereof, so the viewer is challenged to read a face without the benefit of the environmental cues we naturally use to form our interpersonal reactions. All the portraits in this series have been taken from the same angle, with the same equipment, but Scholler's intention is to bring out personality and capture individuality in each subject, searching for a flash of vulnerability and integrity. He adds, the greatest challenge in taking these images lies in the attempt to arrest the subtle moment that flickers between expressions, movements of which the subject is unaware.

_transcript: There's no such thing as an AI artist because AI art is not real art. And watching this video of this dude trying to defend AI art and make excuses for the reason that people do it is just honestly disgusting. Like if I buy a ticket to ride on an airplane, that doesn't make me a pilot. If I type a search into Google, that doesn't make me an author. When I flip on a light switch, it doesn't make me an electrician. If I go buy a pack of muffins, I'm not a baker. Because when you're making AI art, you're not actually doing anything except for sourcing other people's art and doing a poor mashup of it. In a sane world, it would be considered copyright infringement, but we don't live in a sane world. And this guy's excuses make me so mad because he tries to say that because he has ADHD he could never do art. And that some people aren't gifted or talented at art. Well, guess what? Anybody who's an artist, they spent years to decades developing that skill. That's the barrier to entry, is you have to spend time developing the skill. And as somebody who also has ADHD, I find it extremely frustrating that he tries to use that as an excuse of why he couldn't be an artist. Because there's certain art forms that I didn't really have the patience for, I struggled to go back to a painting over and over. I couldn't really do comics because it took so long I would lose interest. So what did I do? I do what everyone else does, and you look for an art that you want to go back to, something that you want to invest your time into. In his video, he talked about how he wanted to be a writer, but he never was able to focus on writing enough to do it. You didn't want to be a writer. You wanted to be an author. You wanted to have a finished work you didn't want to put in the time. Like I'm currently writing a book. Every author in the world doesn't always want to do it. But what you do is you set aside time. And every night at the end of the night I spend 30 minutes to an hour writing my stories Whether I want to or not Whether I having trouble focusing or not Go watch interviews with any famous writer or any kind of artist and they talk about that they don always want to do their art but that doesn't mean that they give themselves the excuse and the out they just do it I was just watching an artist the other day who didn't have arms and he paints with his feet I saw someone who was paralyzed and the only thing they could use was their mouth and so they would bite down on a paintbrush and they would still paint. An artist pushes through their limitations and they do the things that they want to do, whatever the boundary is. And I genuinely am resentful towards all of the people who try to make excuses that they weren't good at art and so that's why they like AI art so much. It's an entitlement because AI art wouldn't exist without sourcing from artists who actually put in the time, from those who overcame those boundaries and still made their art. And this is exactly why it's so disrespectful when people will tell people who do art forms that they're lucky. There's nothing lucky about it. They put the time in and they developed a skill. And that's how skills work. And when I was thinking about making this video, I was like, AI artists are like somebody who reads a cookbook and thinks that they're a chef or somebody that uses Hamburger Helper to make a meal. But that's not even true because when you read a book, at least you did something, right? Even if you just read a cookbook, it doesn't make you a chef, but at least you learned something. If you go and make a meal with Hamburger Helper, you may not have done every step, but you developed skills while you were doing that. You learned some of the process to cooking, but when you go type in a prompt and art gets spit out, you literally did nothing. There's not a single person in the world that was born being able to do art, but when you type a prompt in and you get art out, all you did was take from somebody else.

description: How to tell if youre a true artist
_transcript: This is how you know if someone is a true artist or not. The fact is, in the digital age, with social media and all this other bullshit, so much stuff is becoming, exploding and becoming viral just because it's shocking. And real art is hard to, you know, find these days. A true artist doesn't have a choice. A true artist doesn't want to do it. Doesn't wake up one day and says, I need a new hobby. A true artist has to do it. It doesn't matter what money they make, how many admirers or haters they have. A true artist is built to survive off one thing, and that is their art, right? I had all these other wide-eyed, you know, stars in their eyes, friends, and freaks that I met along the way. And we were all like, oh my god, we're going to do this. We're going to make these things happen that we always dreamt of. And I thought I'd found all these similar people. And as the years went by and failures happened and life happened and time happened these people started to drop away They started to drop off They started to for lack of a better term give up And I found it really hard to understand I found it really difficult to relate to them anymore. When I did start to have success, it was exciting. It was empowering and reassuring. I had lots of people around me start to say oh you're still doing this and it puzzled me made me think oh I guess I am because there is no other choice I have to do it if I don't I drop dead don't open your mouth and breathe you drop dead if you don't drink water you drop dead that's what being an artist feels like if you don't do it, you die. And if I didn't make one more penny off my career, or one more fan, or one more hater, that wouldn't change a damn thing. Because if I don't do it, I die. So when you're out there wading through the bullshit, trying to find stuff that makes you feel something, that's all you need to look for.

description: A silk-covered mannequin was launched into the stratosphere 33 km above Earth in a project that’s part science experiment, part environmental statement, according to its creators. #cnn #space
_transcript: This might look like a Dementor from Harry Potter, but it's actually a silk-covered mannequin sent to the edge of space. It's part of Mission Taroni, an art and science project created by the Dorothy Project and artistic director of Taroni, Maximilian Kanepa. According to the team, the goal is to explore our relationship with the planet, inspired by the overview effect astronauts feel looking back at Earth. The process wasn't a simple one. To make it, the team made an ultra-lightweight human cast, designed the custom silk covering, and mounted it to a carbon fiber rig. They then launched it from the Canadian countryside by balloon into the stratosphere, about 33 kilometers above the surface of Earth. Up there, the sculpture was exposed to sunlight, gravity, and wind. The result? An eerie floating silk figure above the planet. In the age of AI, it was important to the creators that every step of the process was documented, and very little of the final product was edited. While reactions online have been mixed, the creators say they're grateful for the opportunity to have made something never seen before.
